#6580. The Most Unhinged Recipes Ever To Air On Food Network

Your favorite TV chefs have some explaining to do.

Since Food Network launched in 1993, the chefs who grace our screens have shared thousands upon thousands of recipes. Many have become household favorites, the kind we return to for our quick weeknight dinners, fanciful holiday spreads, and everything in between.

But after more than 30 years of cooking on TV, a few recipes are bound to get… a little weird. And some, well, are just completely unhinged. So naturally, we dug through the archives to find some of the strangest recipes ever put on Food Network. Let’s dive in.

Is it outlandish to put chopped hot dogs in your burger patty? Yes, yes it is. Will I still eat it? Absolutely. Rachael mixes the diced hot dogs into the beef with chili powder, Worcestershire, hot sauce, and ketchup, then tops the burger with bacon, cheddar, and a layer of chili sauce. Audacious, yet inspired.

If you think Sandra Lee’s pouring “two shots of vodka” is wild, you may be surprised to learn that the recipe from the viral video is even wilder.

The drink is a muddled radioactive green made by crushing kiwis with melon liqueur and pickled jalapeño juice (and vodka, obviously). Sandra garnishes the drink with a leftover kiwi slice, which immediately and poetically sinks to the bottom. Iconic.

Of all the hundreds of recipes Ree Drummond has filmed for The Pioneer Woman, she's admitted this fried chicken pizza was her least favorite she ever filmed.

Let’s review. The base is frozen bread dough, doused with BBQ sauce, mozzarella, a pile of deli fried chicken strips, dill pickles, and pickled jalapeños, topped with a shocking amount of creamy coleslaw. Wet, fried, and unmistakably American. Your move, Italy.

This is no ordinary lasagna. The noodles are never boiled. They soak in hot water and then line the walls of a 3-quart slow cooker. The eggplant and zucchini are salted, then drained in a salad spinner. Unlike a standard recipe, there's no ricotta and no béchamel.

Instead, the recipe layers beef sausage, ground pork, portobellos, and hand-crushed canned tomatoes with, get this, goat's milk powder. You know, goat’s milk, but powdered—a classic in every American pantry. To top it off, if you want a browned top, the recipe suggests a propane torch. Easy peasy.

Spinach was never meant to be served as a cupcake, and yet here we are. To be fair, the ingredients themselves aren’t too unhinged: Spinach, feta, and cream cheese sound like a pretty pleasant side.

But putting it in a muffin tin, piping on the “frosting,” and calling them cupcakes is another thing entirely. We’re adults. It's okay to admit spinach is tasty without shaping it into dessert.

In theory, I could see someone using polenta instead of rice to make rice pudding. Sure, it might not be good, but it’s at least theoretically possible.

What Sandra has created here, however, is no rice pudding. It is quick-cooking polenta stirred with Parmesan, dried thyme, and, completely inexplicably, white chocolate chips. I’m sorry, but “sweet and salty” can only take you so far.

This recipe is very different from the rest on this list because, well, it's barely a recipe. First, Rachael tells us to put a few mini chocolate chips in the bottom of an ice cream cone to prevent drips. Then we soften the ice cream, scoop it, and serve. And... that's it. That's the entire thing.

One commenter was so inspired by the recipe that they shared one of their own: “I have a similar new recipe for everyone to try. It's called Gum. Open the wrapper and stick it in your mouth.” To Rachael’s credit, it’s at least a meal you can make in under 30 minutes.

Somewhere out there is a person who smiles with unbridled joy when they see honeydew on the fruit plate—Ingrid made this soup in an episode of Simply Delicioso for them and them only. You might think this soup is some sort of green, slightly fruity gazpacho. Oh, how I wish.

This recipe has no olive oil, cucumber, garlic, onion, vinegar, or anything you’d usually find in a Spanish gazpacho. It is just honeydew, sour cream, mint, and some ham. I imagine Ingrid was inspired by prosciutto and melon, but why it is in soup form is a question that will haunt me for a long time.

It’s not easy to get 2.7 stars on a Food Network recipe, but rice with grapes does the trick. Rachael brings dry red wine to a boil, cooks white rice in it, then removes it from the heat and adds raw grapes.

It’s truly incredible how a recipe with only five ingredients can be so uniquely unhinged. As one commenter put it, “This was really good, but I recommend making it without rice or grapes.”

#6577. This Coffee Subscription Delivers Some of the Freshest Beans We’ve Tried

It's one of the best gifts you can give to coffee lovers this holiday season.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

It really doesn't get fresher than this. A Storyville coffee subscription delivers delicious beans right to your doorstep.

We’ve all been there. Standing in the grocery store staring at dozens of coffee brands and trying to decide which one might perk us up, only to end up scowling at a subpar cup of sludge the next morning. Well, those days are over because Storyville, one of Seattle’s best coffee shops, now delivers freshly roasted beans straight to your door.

I tried a Storyville coffee subscription, and I assure you that you’ll never have to waste your time (or money) on stale beans again. Here’s everything you need to know about this caffeinated club.

Storyville is one of the highest-rated coffee shops in Seattle, with locations at Pike Place and at 1st and Madison. They also have a roasting studio you can tour to see exactly where your coffee beans are roasted before making their way to your door. But if you can’t make it to Seattle, they also offer coffee subscription services with nationwide shipping.

The brand sources premium-grade green coffees and roasts each bean varietal individually before blending. Beans are roasted on the darker end of medium and feature a rich, natural sweetness with notes of chocolate and caramel. Unlike many other dark roasts, this coffee has a smooth finish and no bitterness. Best of all, Storyville ships its coffee immediately after roasting.

Storyville subscriptions are highly customizable in order to fit your needs. First, choose between whole beans and single-serve pods. Then choose the quantity and delivery frequency that best suits your needs. You can pause, skip or cancel via text at any time. Moreover, you’ll receive 20% off, among other perks.

I am a coffee fiend. On any given day, I’m three cups in by 9 a.m. That’s why I couldn’t wait to get my hands on a bag of real Seattle coffee.

My order arrived on Wednesday, October 28. I received a bag of Prologue coffee beans, Sunrise espresso beans and Epilogue decaf coffee beans. I knew the roast dates would be stamped on the bags, but I was amazed to see that my beans had been roasted just days prior, on October 25 and October 27. Talk about fresh!

I opened the Prologue first and poured the entire bag into the bean hopper of my De’Longhi Rivelia. After brewing, I took a sip before adding my cream and sugar and was amazed by how smooth it was. It was fresh and flavorful without a hint of bitterness. I love a dark roast and could drink this all day long.

The next day, I opened the Sunrise espresso beans. I used it to make a regular cup of coffee followed by an Americano. Like the Prologue, the beans were clearly fresh, and the coffee was exceptionally smooth! I’ll be saving this bag along with the decaf for espresso martinis with my girlfriends.

As a dark roast gal, I’ve had my fair share of coffee that tastes bitter or burnt. I didn’t get any notes of bitterness from Storyville coffee. I’ll also point out that a bag of Prologue coffee lasted one week. Given how much coffee I drink plus the fact that my husband tends to make a cup here and there, I’m not surprised we went through it so quickly. Luckily, the subscription is completely customizable. If you drink as much coffee as I do, you’ll want to order two or three bags at a time. But if you just enjoy one cup per day, then one bag at a time will suffice.

That said, these beans are so fresh we wouldn’t be surprised if you start drinking more coffee than usual. And we certainly wouldn’t blame you!

It’s also easy to send a subscription as a gift. Simply head over to their gifting page and opt for three, five, eight or 12 prepaid shipments.

Each of Earth's hemispheres experiences summer, but how do they differ?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Each year, Earth's Northern and Southern hemispheres cycle through four seasons, including summer.

Given that the hemispheres are symmetric about the equator, you may think that, on both sides of the world, summers should be similar – both in terms of their climate and factors like their length. But are Northern and Southern hemisphere summers really the same?

Climate experts tell Live Science that they differ quite a bit — and that comes with a clear recommendation for sun enthusiasts.

The most obvious difference is that Northern and Southern summers happen at different times. According to NASA, this arises because Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of our planet's orbit around the sun.

This tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to be oriented toward the sun at different times throughout the year. Between the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice and autumnal equinox, the Northern Hemisphere is oriented toward the sun, resulting in summer, and vice versa in the Southern Hemisphere.

This means that summers between the Northern and Southern hemispheres sit six months out of sync with each other — with Northern summers spanning late June to late September and Southern ones going from late December to late March. (Summers are also defined meteorologically, or relative to changes in weather phenomena, as being the hottest months of the year. Under this definition, Northern summers run from June to August, and Southern ones go from December to February.)

Another difference between Northern and Southern summers is their duration. According to NASA, Northern Hemisphere summers are, on average, 4.5 days longer than Southern Hemisphere summers. (This is with respect to the astronomical definition; meteorologically, Northern summers are longer than Southern ones by two days in non-leap years, but this is due to February being the calendar's shortest month.)

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The 4.5-day difference occurs because Earth's orbit around the sun is slightly elliptical instead of perfectly circular, according to NASA. Consequently, Earth's orbital velocity (the speed at which our planet hurtles around the sun) isn't constant.

Earth isn't the only planet that experiences such a dichotomy in the duration of seasons. According to NASA, Mars does too: Northern summers on the Red Planet are 24 Martian days — 24.66 Earth days — longer than the planet's Southern Hemisphere's summers. This greater difference is because Mars's orbit is much more oval-shaped than Earth's.

During the Northern Hemisphere's summer, Earth is farther away from the sun and thus moving more slowly, said Georg Feulner, a senior researcher at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. This is due to Kepler's second law of planetary motion, he added.

This means that at aphelion ‪(the point at which our planet is farthest from the sun)‬ Earth is traveling at 18.2 miles per second (29.3 kilometers per second). This jumps to 18.82 miles per second (30.29 km/s) at perihelion ‪(the point when Earth is closest to the sun ) which occurs during Southern summers.

While this may seem like a tiny difference in speed, it causes our planet's path around the sun to be 53,686 miles (86,400 kilometers) shorter in a 24-hour-interval at aphelion compared with at perihelion. In other words, Earth covers more "ground" at aphelion than at perihelion over a 24-hour-interval. "Therefore, the time between the Northern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes is longer than the time between the Southern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes, Feulner told Live Science in an email.

A third point of difference is that Northern summers are typically hotter than Southern ones. A 2015 study in the journal Climate Dynamics showed the precise value of this depends on whether temperatures are measured on the surface air, land or ocean, and the latitude at which they're taken. Nonetheless, when averaged over all domains and latitudes, Northern summers are 7.83 degrees Fahrenheit (4.35 degrees Celsius) hotter than Southern ones.

So what's behind this? Earth's changing distance from the sun isn't important. If it were, Earth's aphelion crossing during Northern summers should make them cooler than Southern summers during the perihelion crossing. Instead, several other factors are responsible.

One is the Northern Hemisphere's bigger fraction of land compared to its large water bodies like oceans. "Land has a lower heat capacity than water and so increases temperature more for a given heating than water does," Richard Seager, a professor at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, told Live Science in an email. As a result, the many inland sites in the Northern Hemisphere heat up rapidly and have higher summer temperatures, according to the UCAR Center for Science Education.

Additionally, Seager said, another difference lies in the way heat is distributed through air and water. The solar heat that land receives warms only the first few feet of the atmosphere, while the heat water absorbs gets mixed throughout its depths. This makes the Southern Hemisphere — with its larger fraction of water — cooler over summer.

The second factor for the North Hemisphere's higher summer temperatures are cross-equatorial ocean currents. Such currents cross the equator, transferring water and heat between the hemispheres. The primary current is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC). "The AMOC transports heat from the SH [Southern Hemisphere] to the NH in the Atlantic," Feulner said. This warms Northern oceans and seas, which, in turn, heats up adjacent land-masses.

So, Northern Hemisphere summers are longer and hotter than Southern ones. If you want to stretch out your summer, you now know where to go.

#6574. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6573. This Old-School Drink Is Making a Comeback for the Coziest Winter Cocktails

Port isn't just for sipping after dinner. We asked a respected winemaker about how this rich, fruity wine can be used to make easy winter cocktails.

For my birthday, a friend gifted me a bottle of Angel’s Envy bourbon. It was a fantastic gift (thank you, Jaclyn!), but what stood out to me was a detail on the label: “finished in port wine barrels.”

Usually I hear of bourbon barrels being used to age other things. The Goose Island Bourbon County Stout, for example, is a beer that’s aged in bourbon barrels, and it’s so special that people will line up outside grocery stores in the hope of grabbing a pack. But I’m less familiar with port wine, and I wanted to learn more.

I’ve been seeing port pop up on menus and in cocktail recipes with more frequency. When I think of port, I imagine the nobility in medieval times sipping from big pewter goblets. Of course, you don’t need to be a royal to enjoy it!

I reached out to an expert for some advice on how to incorporate port into more of my winter cocktails. He gave me a crash course in everything I needed to know about the wine, and shared some of the best ways to use it in cocktails.

I connected with David Guimaraens, head winemaker for Taylor Fladgate. Born in Portugal, David is the sixth generation of his family to be involved in the port business. He’s widely recognized as one of the most gifted winemakers in the modern port industry, and his tips on how to winterize cocktails with port are simple enough to incorporate into any cocktail routine.

Taste of Home: For someone who may be unfamiliar with the category, how would you explain what port is and what distinguishes it from other styles of wine?

David Guimaraens: Port is a fortified wine produced in Portugal’s Douro Valley, one of the world’s oldest demarcated wine regions. What sets it apart is that a small amount of grape spirit is added during fermentation. This stops the fermentation process so some of the natural sweetness from the grapes remains in the finished product. The result is a uniquely rich, concentrated fruit wine with an incredible depth of flavor.

There are many different styles of port, from fresh, vibrant ruby ports to complex, aged tawnies and exceptional vintage ports. That diversity makes port a far more versatile category than many people realize, with styles suited to everything from cocktails and aperitifs to food pairings and after-dinner enjoyment.

TOH: What qualities does port bring to a mixed drink, and why does it work particularly well as a cocktail ingredient?

DG: Port brings fruit notes, sweetness and complexity to a cocktail. Depending on the style, its flavor profile can range from fresh berry and spice to dried fruit, nuts and caramel. It is remarkably versatile behind the bar. Port can replace or complement vermouth and other sweet components in classic cocktails. Its concentration of flavor allows you to add complexity to a drink without a long list of ingredients.

TOH: Why is port trending for winter cocktails and seasonal entertaining?

DG: There is something naturally comforting about port during the colder months. Its fruit and spice notes pair particularly well with seasonal flavors such as cranberry, orange, cinnamon, ginger and chocolate, making it a versatile choice for holiday entertaining. Port has also always been a wine for sharing. Serving it in a cocktail or a simple spritz offers a more informal, contemporary way to enjoy that tradition and bring port to the table.

TOH: For someone experimenting with port cocktails at home for the first time, what is the easiest way to begin? Are there simple serves, ratios or ingredient pairings you recommend?

DG: Keep it simple. You don’t need to be a mixologist to make a great port cocktail. A port spritz is an easy place to start: Serve port over plenty of ice, top with sparkling water or tonic, and finish with a slice or twist of fresh citrus. It is refreshing, simple to prepare and easy to adapt to your own taste.

TOH: For consumers shopping for port to use in cocktails, what should they look for when selecting a bottle? Does someone need to invest in an expensive Port to make a great cocktail?

DG: Absolutely not. In fact, I would reserve great vintage ports for enjoying on their own!

For cocktails, look for a good-quality, fruit-driven reserve ruby port with enough character to stand up alongside the other ingredients. Fonseca Bin 27 is a great example: It is approachable and full of rich berry fruit, and it has the structure and depth to work extremely well in cocktails.

Have you made port cocktails before? Let us know your favorite version in the comments below!

#6572. These Wine Glasses Are the Only Ones That Can Survive My Clumsiness

I spent years living with roommates and making due with our collective assortment of mismatched dishware, throwing washed take-out containers haphazardly into a cupboard and reusing them until they were cracked and stained, and living with a pantry that was in a constant state of moderate disarray. But when I moved in with my boyfriend, I took the opportunity to get my shit together. I pride myself on being a relatively put-together person, and that now translates to my kitchen too. I’ve got a cabinet full of well-organized food storage containers with their corresponding lids, I keep my spices neatly stacked in deli containers with labeled with color-coded kitchen tape, I replaced my chipped water glasses with a matching set, and I have a special drawer that houses the linens, taper candles, and flatware I pull out when I’m hosting. It all feels very adult.

Until recently, though, there was one remaining aspect of my kitchen that still needed help. While I have more fun coupes and rocks glasses than I know what to do with, I haven’t owned a matching set of wine glasses since college—in fact, at the time of my move, I had two left to my name. It’s not for lack of trying: I’ve tested out glassware during my time at BA, bringing home countless options in the hopes that they’d be my forever stems. I’ve somehow managed to break every single one of them, which has become a running joke for those that know me.

But despite my clumsiness, I’m not willing to sacrifice style for durability. I want a thin-stemmed, thin-rimmed, elegant wine glass that won’t snap in two the minute I lay my hands on it. Is that too much to ask?

For the longest time, I thought it might be, and had resigned myself to sipping wine out of stemless tumblers—until I discovered Gabriel-Glas’s StandArt All Purpose Wine Glass. They’ve got a sleek, slightly conical shape that I find enhances reds, whites, and rosés alike, with a slight curve between the bowl and the rim that adds a touch of personality to an otherwise classic silhouette. The stem is thin enough to satisfy my desire for elegance without being so delicate that I’m scared I’ll snap it, and the laser-cut rim is a joy to sip from.

Because the glasses are machine-blown from a single piece of molten crystal, they have none of the weak points that tend to form where traditional multipart glasses are joined. The machine-blown construction also keeps the cost per glass low enough that I won’t mind replacing one if (let’s be real, when) I do drop and shatter it. But I’m pleased to report that as of right now, all six of my beloved StandArt glasses are intact and ready to take on my new apartment’s first season of holiday hosting and cozy weather hangs. Bring on the winter reds and festive bottles of bubbly.

The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.

The Hubble Space Telescope's optical light view of the Cat's Head Nebula.

Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in near-infrared light.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in mid-infrared light.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6569. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6568. 14 Appetizers That You Can (& Should!) Eat For Dinner

An apps-olutely delicious way to do dinner.

If you’re like me, sometimes you don’t want to make a whole big meal for dinner. A homemade dinner can feel daunting, but I’ll never turn down the opportunity to indulge in appetizers. While it may be frowned upon (though I’d argue wrongfully so) to fill up on pigs in a blanket, stuffed mushrooms, or other finger-food favorites, there are a ton of fantastic appetizers that verge on dinner. It’s those beauties that I turn to for my favorite kinds of evenings: appetizers for dinner! With that in mind, I gathered 14 of our best apps that can (and should) be eaten for dinner. Plus, if you make a few of these on the same night, you’ve got a veritable feast.

Aside from the buttery biscuits, melty provolone cheese, and salty roast beef combo, we’re obsessed with these French dip stuffed biscuits because of how easy (emphasis on easy) they are to make.

These sliders are inspired by a classic fried chicken Caesar salad. They have all the nostalgic flavor notes you love, from crispy fried chicken to a tangy buttermilk dressing.

We love chicken wings in all shapes, sizes, and flavors, but there’s something extra special about the saucy, sweet, savory, and slightly sticky teriyaki wing. Our version skips the store-bought sauce in favor of a few pantry staples that come together in just a few minutes to create a gingery, garlicky soy-based sauce that clings to oven-baked wings and never falls short on flavor.

These old-school sausage pinwheels are a classic for a reason. They feature crescent dough with bits of sausage and red pepper layered within a creamy garlic cheese spread. Bell pepper + cream cheese + cheddar cheese make for a pimento-inspired bite.

What’s better than a tray of cheesy chicken nachos? Four cheese chicken nachos! Don’t worry, though, a couple cans of chopped green chiles cut the richness of all that cheese. We’ll leave the toppings up to you, but we suggest The Works, aka red onion, radishes, avocado, jalapeño, cilantro, and hot sauce.

This recipe has everything you could ever want in the seafood classic: They're golden, crispy, and chock-full of crab flavor. Ready in 30 minutes and served with homemade tartar sauce, they are the perfect easy main or low-effort appetizer.

Sheet-pan quesadillas are easy to assemble and fun to customize to your mood. We were inspired here by our French onion pot roast. In both recipes, we’re utilizing French onion soup packets to get that iconic flavor—no caramelizing onions required.

If you aren’t familiar with the muffuletta sandwich, you should be. It’s filled with three different cured meats, a plethora of olives, roasted red peppers, and other brined ingredients. It’s big and proud, and this dip is the perfect scoopable version of it.

If the best wing flavor and sauce combination is hot Buffalo wings and ranch dip, then it stands to reason that a ranch wing with hot Buffalo dip would be equally delicious—right? Damn right. We flipped the classic combo to create a ranch-flavored chicken wing served with a side of zesty, spicy Buffalo sauce.

This Nashville hot chicken dip brings the heat and MORE. Beware—this party dip is for major spice fans only. A cream cheese, mayo, and sour cream base meets hot sauce and breaded chicken for a spicy, creamy dip that is also perfectly filling.

These sliders are the crème de la crème. Ham, Swiss, and jammy caramelized onions are layered between the star of the show: buttery and soft Hawaiian rolls. You simply split the rolls, layer them, bake, and in a little over 10 minutes, you'll have a dozen hot, mind-blowing sandwiches ready to serve.

Caul us crazy, but we believe that these cauliflower wings are just as good as regular wings. This recipe transforms this staple veggie into crispy, golden bites that were made to be drenched in your favorite sauce.

These vegan potstickers are easy to put together and most of your time is spent roasting your squash until really tender, which can be done ahead of time. Crimping takes a little practice, but the good news is that even if they look a little wonky they are still going to taste great!

In these Buffalo chicken meatballs, ground chicken is formed into meatballs with bread crumbs and plenty of seasoning, before being drenched in the signature hot Buffalo sauce. Ready in 30 minutes, these meatballs are a flavor-packed app you can have ready in no time.

#6567. Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies Treats

Recipe by Cori Cooper, flagstaff, Arizona

Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats are party-ready, from the bright rainbow colors and fruity flavor to the crisp, chewy texture and marshmallow pull.

If there are Rice Krispies treats on any table full of treats, I’ll make a beeline for them before even glancing at brownies or cupcakes. The combination of light, crisp cereal and chewy marshmallow hits every time. There will always be a place in my heart for the classic ones, but playing around with different Rice Krispies treats variations brings me endless joy. Cori Cooper, a Community Cook from Flagstaff, Arizona, feels the same way, which led her to create these colorful Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats.

By just switching to a rainbow-colored, fruity cereal, Cori transformed the dessert without changing the beloved texture of the original or making it too sweet. I’ll be making these for my next bake sale. Hopefully they make it out of my kitchen!

Place the cereal and half of one package of mini marshmallows in a large bowl.

In a microwave-safe bowl or a large saucepan over low heat, melt the remaining marshmallows in butter, stirring until they’re smooth. Stir in the salt, if using it, then remove the mixture from the heat. Pour it over the cereal mixture.

Editor’s Tip: If using the microwave, heat the butter and marshmallows in 30- to 45-second intervals, stirring in between, to prevent the butter from getting too hot and splattering.

Press into a lightly greased 8-inch square baking pan using waxed paper or a lightly greased spatula. Let the mixture cool to room temperature. Cut it into bars.

Editor’s Tip: For bars that hold together but still have an airy bite and chewy texture, press the cereal mixture evenly into the pan, but don’t use all your might and pack them in.

Store Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats at room temperature, tightly wrapped, for three to five days. Technically, they last longer, but the cereal will start to get stale and the treats will become brittle over time. You can leave the treats in the baking pan and tightly wrap the entire pan, or transfer cut squares to an airtight food storage container, adding a piece of parchment between layers to keep them from sticking together.

You can freeze Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats for up to six weeks, but they won’t have the same soft, stretchy texture as freshly made treats. Pack the treats in a freezer-proof food storage bag, pressing out the excess air, or place them in a container with an airtight lid, adding a piece of parchment between the layers. They will thaw quickly, so just let them stand at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes before eating them.

Cereal treats can end up hard instead of soft, stretchy and chewy if the marshmallows are stale or overheated, or if you pack the treats too tightly into the baking dish. Stale marshmallows don’t have the same moisture and bounce as fresh ones, making them tough from the start. And since marshmallows are mostly sugar, they can burn or become candy-like if overcooked, which makes the treats unpleasantly firm. If you compress the cereal too much, you crush out all its air, which results in dense treats that are hard to bite through.

You can use several different pans for these Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats to vary their shape or thickness. For thinner treats, press the cereal mixture into a 9-inch square baking pan. For a different shape, use an 8-inch or 9-inch round cake pan and then cut the cereal treats into triangles, like slices of pie.

Since these are Fruity Pebbles treats, you should keep at least half the amount of Fruity Pebbles, but if you’re a few cups short (this happens to me all the time), you can make up the difference with one of the best childhood cereals, like Cheerios or Lucky Charms. You can use almost any crisp, puffed or flaked cereal, but consider what will taste the best with the fruity base. I’d recommend a cereal with light sweetness and a nutty or vanilla flavor so you don’t overshadow the Fruity Pebbles.

#6566. Spiced and Glazed Roast Turkey

Our mission: A roast turkey that’s boldly spiced, beautifully glazed, and—can we type this loudly enough?—PROPERLY COOKED. That means juicy breast meat, tender dark meat, and plenty of deeply browned skin. Andy Baraghani and Brad Leone’s solution? Break the bird into five pieces: two wings, two legs, and one whole breast. Roasting the bird in parts gives you more control over when each piece is done—no dry breast meat or tough legs.

They didn’t slouch on flavor either. A peppery dry brine with garlic powder, onion powder, and smoked paprika gets to work 24–48 hours before the turkey goes into the oven. Then comes the glaze: a savory-tangy mix of soy sauce, vinegar, brown sugar, orange zest, and herbs. Brushed onto the turkey as it roasts, it builds a glossy, deeply burnished finish. And because the pieces cook on a wire rack set inside a baking sheet, you get more exposed skin for browning and a more even cook overall.

If the idea of doing surgery on a raw turkey gives you a stress rash, ask your butcher to do it—even at the supermarket. Request a 12–14-lb. turkey cut into five pieces, with the thighs attached to the drumsticks, the breast left whole, and the backbone removed. If they ask why, just say: Yes, you’re making that ridiculous Bon Appétit recipe. If you’d rather do the honors yourself, here’s our guide to breaking down a whole turkey.

Choose an unbrined turkey for this recipe. Many supermarket birds are already treated with a salt solution, sometimes labeled “self-basting,” “enhanced,” or “contains a solution.” Adding this dry brine on top can make the turkey overly salty. Check the packaging before you buy.

Should I rinse off the dry brine before roasting?

No. Leave the seasoning on the turkey when you coat it with oil. Some of the spice mixture may rub off, but that’s fine. There’s no need to rinse the bird, and washing raw poultry can spread bacteria around your kitchen.

Can I use the pan drippings to make gravy?

Yes, but taste them first. Between the seasoned dry brine and soy-based glaze, the drippings can be quite salty and intensely flavored. Use them sparingly and taste your gravy before adding more salt. For a simpler option, try our Make-Ahead Gravy, which doesn’t require drippings at all.

Read our guide to turkey cooking times, no matter the bird’s size or your preferred cooking method.

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 24 hours dry-brining

Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck and giblets removed, breast side up, on a cutting board and pat dry. Grip a wing and pull it outward so you can see where it attaches to the body. Using a sharp boning or chef’s knife, cut through the joint to separate the wing from the breast (if you hit bone, you’re in the wrong spot; pull the wing out farther to help you get into the place where the joint meets the socket). Remove wing; repeat on the other side.

Cut through skin connecting 1 leg to carcass. Pull leg back until the ball joint pops out of its socket; cut through the joint to separate leg. Repeat on the other side.

Now for the breast: Position the turkey breast side down with the opening facing you. Using kitchen shears, cut along one side of backbone until you get all the way through the neck end, then turn the turkey 180° and cut through the other side to remove the backbone (save it for making stock).

Very finely grind 2 Tbsp. whole black peppercorns and 2 Tbsp. whole pink or black peppercorns in a spice mill or mortar and pestle; transfer to a medium bowl. Add ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 Tbsp. garlic powder, 2 Tbsp. onion powder, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1 Tbsp. smoked paprika, and use your fingers to mix together.

Place turkey pieces, skin side up, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet. Sprinkle salt mixture liberally all over turkey, patting to adhere. You may not need all of it, but it’s good to have extra since some will end up on the baking sheet. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 24 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil to make cleanup easy and set rack back inside. Arrange turkey pieces on rack, skin side up, and let sit at room temperature up to 2 hours to help decrease the cooking time.

Meanwhile, cook small handful of hardy herbs (such as sage, rosemary, bay leaves, and/or thyme), 4 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, ⅓ cup low-sodium soy sauce, ⅓ cup (packed; 71 g) light brown sugar, and ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until sugar is dissolved and glaze thickens slightly (it should just barely coat a spoon), 10–12 minutes. Remove glaze from heat.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Rub turkey with 6 Tbsp. neutral oil (such as vegetable, peanut, or canola) and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet. Roast turkey, rotating baking sheet halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown, 20–25 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 20 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast registers 150°, and 170° when inserted into the thickest part of the thighs, 50–70 minutes longer (total cooking time will be 1–1½ hours). Skin should be deep golden brown and shiny. Transfer turkey to a cutting board; tent loosely with foil. Let rest 30–60 minutes before carving.

#6564. Peppermint Bark Cookie Bars

Line a 13×9-inch pan with parchment paper, letting the ends extend up the sides. In a large bowl, use a hand mixer or stand mixer to cream the butter, sugar and vanilla extract until it’s light and fluffy, five to seven minutes. Beat in the egg yolks until they’re combined.

In another bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour and salt. Gradually beat the flour mixture into the creamed mixture just until no streaks of flour remain.

In the top of a double boiler or a metal bowl over hot water, melt the dark chocolate, stirring until it’s completely smooth. Remove the bowl from the heat and spread the dark chocolate over the cooled bars.

Editor’s Tip: Never let the water touch the bottom of the bowl, or it will burn the chocolate. Also, try not to get any water into the chocolate, or it will seize.

Repeat the melting and spreading process with the white chocolate, then immediately sprinkle the top with crushed peppermint candies while the chocolate is still wet.

Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6561. These Panera Snowman Cups Are Only Available for a Day—Here’s How to Get One

The Panera Snowman Cup is giving the Starbucks Bearista Cup some cozy competition. Here's what you need to know about the limited-edition mystery boxes.

I don’t generally need an incentive to stop at Panera in December. Any of those delicious soups in a bread bowl is a fairly convincing argument on its own. But this year, the chain is giving us another reason to visit: collectible glass snowman cups, with a chance to get one free.

If you’ve been admiring the Starbucks Bearista cup, these little snowmen might also deserve a spot on your wish list. Panera’s version comes in a mystery box containing one of two designs, naughty or nice. The free cup offer runs on Dec. 3, and with only 12 available at each participating cafe, there are a few details to keep in mind before you go.

The limited-edition glass cups come in two designs inspired by the naughty-and-nice theme of Panera’s holiday packaging. Each mystery box holds one snowman cup, so you won’t know which you’ve received until you open it.

There are also a few new things to drink while you admire your cute cup. Panera’s new holiday menu, rolling out this week, includes peppermint white mocha and pistachio white mocha beverages. Both flavors are available as a latte, iced coffee or Frozen Java, finished with peppermint bark pieces or pistachio pieces. The iced coffees have sweet cream cold foam, and the lattes and Frozen Java drinks get whipped cream.

On Dec. 3, the first 12 customers at each participating U.S. cafe who make a qualifying purchase of $25 or more will receive a free Snowman Cup, while supplies last. There’s a limit of one per person, so you may want to make that Panera outing a breakfast date.

You’ll need to order inside the cafe at the cashier. Kiosk, Rapid Pick-Up, drive-thru, catering and delivery orders—including those placed through third-party sites—don’t qualify.

If you don’t get your hands on one of those first 12 boxes, you’ll have another way to find a snowman. A limited number of cups will also be available through the Panera Shop for $22 each. An online sale date hasn’t been announced yet, so keep an eye on the shop if you’re hoping to grab one.

Are you going to be first in line at Panera on Dec. 3? Let us know in the comments below!

#6559. I’m So Obsessed With This Coffee Mug, I Tell Strangers About It

I wouldn't call myself a minimalist by any means, but I am not someone who buys a lot of kitchen gadgets or rushes to snag the latest seasonal cup. But ever since I picked up my first Fellow Carter Move Mug five years ago, I’ve happily repurchased it several times.

This sleek little mug, designed by the coffee nerds at Fellow, keeps your brew hot (or cold) without sacrificing flavor. I use it so often that I’ve sung its praises to a coffee shop owner in Washington, a bed-and-breakfast proprietor in Maine, and countless other strangers.

I love this mug more than I can express—so much, in fact, that I reached out to Fellow founder, Jake Miller, to chat about it. He launched the brand 13 years ago with the goal of delivering great design to coffee brewing, but customers kept asking for an exceptional way to drink their coffee on the go. So a company founded by and for coffee obsessives made the ultimate companion container.

The Carter Move Mug is designed with a superior drinking experience in mind. The body of the mug tapers into a thin drinking lip that Miller said was inspired by a wine glass. When you take a sip, you’re touching metal and not paint, and the lip is protected when the mug is closed.

At the time, other to-go cups were designed with a small opening in the lid and completely missed out on the aromatics. “It was a pretty opinionated design choice, but we wanted people to experience the incredible smells of coffee,” he explained. “Once the lid is off, you have this really great drinking experience.” While the lip of the mug is metal, the inside of the mug is ceramic-coated, so it doesn’t impart any taste to the coffee. According to Miller, “that allows for a more pure expression of the coffee.”

When I tell people about the Carter Mug, I like to joke that it’s almost too good at its job. Hot drinks stay very hot for hours, and I regularly find ice in the mug a full day after I first made my chilled version. I once left a mug of hot coffee in a car during a blizzard, and after almost a day, the coffee was still pleasant to drink. Miller said this effective temperature control is from two things: the distance between the two walls and how much vacuum insulation the mug has. Also, Fellow designed the lid to be gasket-tight so there’s minimal heat loss.

One of my favorite features of the Move Mug is the splash guard that clicks into the vessel and prevents big spills while you’re drinking in motion. (As a person prone to mess, this is very helpful.) This element, along with some other accessories, was born out of feedback based on how customers use their mugs, including a straw for cold coffee, a cup holder-friendly size, and the option for a slide top lid. “Everything we do is customer-driven,” Miller noted.

Maybe not important to how your coffee tastes — but important to aesthetics — the Move Mug is sleek and sophisticated, which means it’s suitable for most situations. There’s a nice range of colors, and it looks great in my hand on my commute and on my desk in the office. It’s truly the perfect accessory.

#6558. This Home Locker Made My Entryway So Much More Functional

Mustard Made home lockers blend utilitarian functionality and bold color for the perfect entryway and mudroom furniture.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I’m always on the hunt for products that nail the sweet spot between form and function. And with a toddler at home, let’s just say we’ve accumulated stuff. Toys, shoes, kid gear, you name it. Our entryway, laundry room and pretty much every shared space could use a little organizational intervention.

So, when I first saw Mustard Made lockers online, I was intrigued. The bold colors and playful, schoolhouse-inspired design, coupled with the range of sizes, made them feel like a storage upgrade with personality. I was looking for a compact catch-all near the front door for the shoes, hats and everyday essentials we’re constantly grabbing on our way out.

The more I thought about it, the more I liked the idea of a home locker: sturdy metal, magnetic doors and an easy-to-clean finish. Sold. I ordered the two-door Midi locker from Mustard.

Of course, choosing a color was a whole ordeal. I played it safe with Chalk, expecting a crisp white, but it turned out to be more of a warm off-white. It’s not quite what I pictured, but it works in our space. That said, if I could do it all over again, I’d tell myself to be bold and go with Mustard or Olive.

Here’s how the locker came together, how it’s holding up and whether it’s helping tame the everyday chaos.

A utilitarian storage cabinet that pairs versatile functionality with a pop of color

The Midi arrived on my porch in a flat, narrow box that was easy to lift and carry where I needed to build it. Once I unpacked everything, I was happy to find that most of the locker simply slots and clicks into place. No tools, screws or complicated assembly required. The only tool I needed was a Phillips-head screwdriver to attach the door handles.

Mustard Made includes printed instructions, and you can also find them on the website, along with a step-by-step assembly video if you need a little extra guidance.

The trickiest part? Getting the doors on. They can take a bit of fiddling, but gently bending the small tab helps hold the L-shaped bracket in place and keeps the door steady while you assemble it.

Once assembled, the locker feels solid, sturdy and made to last. But it’s the brand’s attention to detail that really makes it functional. There are attachment points on the back for securing it to the wall (a welcome feature with a toddler around), interior hooks on each door for hanging smaller items, adjustable shelves and even a cable hole in the back for managing cords.

And the customization options are a bonus, even though they’re sold separately. Mustard Made sells extra shelves, super-strong button magnets and metal hangers for the Skinny and Twinny lockers, which can double as mini wardrobes. They also offer adorable alphabet and number magnets for displaying messages, labeling spaces or giving older kids something to play with.

Another thing I love? Mustard Made offers six different locker styles and sizes, so there’s an option for just about every room and organizational storage need.

My daughter loves using the locker as a little art gallery, proudly displaying her masterpieces. And it’s not just for artwork. The home locker is a fun spot for handwritten notes, photos, collectible magnets and other little things we want to put on display. The Mustard Made button magnets are surprisingly strong and sturdy, too, holding much more than your average fridge magnet.

If you have things you want to keep under lock and key, Mustard Made has you covered. Each locker door comes with its own lock and set of keys. It took me a little while to realize that the locks are different, so a heads-up: each door comes with two keys, and you’ll want to keep them organized. Mixing them up (or losing them altogether) could lead to frustration.

In our house, the locker is primarily a shoe drop zone by the front door, so we haven’t had much reason to use the locks. But I can see this feature coming in handy for storing valuables or keeping potentially hazardous household items out of little hands. Just be sure to use appropriate child-safety measures for anything that poses a risk.

With so many shapes, sizes and colors to choose from, Mustard Made lockers are a versatile storage solution for just about any room. Think mudrooms, laundry rooms, playrooms, entryways, porches and beyond.

They’re not limited to hiding clutter, either. Depending on the style and size, they can pull double duty as entertainment consoles, wardrobes, buffet tables or even drink cabinets. Basically, they’re as flexible as they are functional.

A colorful home locker for your entryway, mudroom, playroom, garage, porch and beyond

You can shop the Midi and the full range of lockers directly from Mustard Made. The Midi retails for $369 and comes in 12 colors. Want something a little more design-forward? The brand also offers lockers with fluted glass doors for a more elevated look.

#6557. How a Jungle Farm in the Yucatán Is Transforming Its Maya Community

“The future is ancestral,” said Gonzalo Samaranch Granados. “Mayans were very good observers of the sky, but also the jungle and its complex relationship of plants and animals.” The rainy season, when farming deep in the Yucatán jungle proves more challenging than usual, had ended, and he was preparing for the next growing cycle, when the garden beds at Mestiza de Indias, a 550-acre reserve and biodiversity lab, would once again sprout heirloom tomatoes, eggplant, carrots, kale, garlic, herbs—crops popular with restaurant and chef collaborators on the Riviera Maya—as well as indigenous varieties with deep cultural significance for the local Mayan community.

Mak’ulan (pepperleaf), pepitas, and maize form the base of the kots’ob tamales prepared by market stall women in the nearby town of Espita. Cempasúchil (marigolds) decorate altars during Día de Muertos. Tomatillos milperos (purple tomatillos) introduced from Hidalgo are added to sikil p’aak and sopa de lima. Samaranch selects and saves native seeds, but he also sources from organic seed companies such as Baker’s Creek and Kitazawa. He’s currently on the hunt for wild ts’unu’un p’aak, or hummingbird tomatoes, a variety endemic to the Yucatán.

Other passion projects at Mestiza de Indias include the cultivation of rare Maya vanilla orchids and the extraction of a citrusy honey produced by endangered Melipona bees. (Ancient Mayans were avid apiarists. Ah Muzen Kab, the Maya god of bees, is featured in the 1,100-year-old Madrid Codex, which also contains detailed instructions for beekeeping.) Next to a ts’iits’il che’ tree where orchid vines twined, Samaranch walked into a screened enclosure protecting square wood boxes that serve as hives for these stingless bees. He removed the top of one to reveal treasure: Instead of combs, the bees create waxen pods, oozing amber-hued honey. It’s never a lot, so every precious taste is bittersweet. Equally important, they are critical pollinators for tropical ecosystems and go crazy for the nectar of ts’iits’il che’ blossoms, which flower after the first rainfall after the dry season. “What we do is possible because I was fascinated by traditional Mayan agriculture,” said Samaranch, a native of Barcelona who traded the art world for regenerative farming. “It’s not only making food. This system is related to culture, medicine, spirituality. It’s about living in harmony with nature, a respectful system.”

This Mesoamerican worldview is known as the milpa. In the Yucatán, it refers to the symbiotic planting of corn, beans, and squashes, often called the Three Sisters, on small-acre farms. (Other Indigenous growers consider sunflowers or bee balm the fourth sister. And when watermelon was introduced to the New World in the 16th century, it was adopted as a sister, too.) The concept of caring for the land, putting back more than you take, replenishing waterways, and reviving heritage crops manifests differently across continents and climates, but it exists wherever farming communities still observe old and slow ways.

By adapting these polyculture techniques into a regenerative project, Samaranch is transforming both the land and its people, including the way they look at the culture of food itself. And he’s not alone: In Australia’s Far East Gippsland, Bruce Pascoe founded Black Duck Foods to perpetuate Aboriginal land-management traditions. Black Duck: A Year at Yumburra is his manifesto about caring for country but also a personal reclamation after devastating bushfires and the loss of elders.At Royal Queen Farms in Acadia Parish, Louisiana, artist and land steward Michelle Joan Papillion has created a food sovereignty network for her community while protecting species native to the region. Johnny Ortiz-Concha and his wife, Maida Branch, bring people together around a communal table at /shed, a subscription supper club that consciously celebrates their ancestry and ecosystem. Menus are based on the crops and livestock they raise or forage at their ranch outside Taos Pueblo. They are custodians of a landrace variety of blue corn known as Tu-ah-tah, gifted to the couple by Ortiz-Concha’s family.

For those who work at Mestiza des Indias, change also starts close to home. The reserve lies almost four miles down a rough track outside the Mayan village of San Pedro Chenchelá, where most residents still live in primitive casa de huano, or mud-daubed wooden houses thatched with palm, and wear brightly patterned huipils, the distinctive Mayan tunic that predates Hispanic fashions. Hiking on foot to the milpa, field-workers have to beware of jaguars, rattlesnakes, and even poisonous trees.

During high season, Samaranch presently employs about 10 workers, most of them women whose husbands commute to the coast for tourism-related jobs. Others leave for bigger cities. Because family members can be away from home for extended periods, this has disrupted the ancestral rhythm of life. And when they do return to the community, it’s often with addiction problems. Even deep in the Yucatán jungle, the arrival of methamphetamine has devastated the region’s younger generation.

To counter this cultural disruption, Samaranch’s Mayan wife, Martha Elena Chan Tuz, a community project leader and former municipal tourism secretary, launched a complementary initiative, forming a cooperative of local needlework crafters who hand embroider table linens with intricate xookbil chuy, or cross-stitches. Their exquisite dinner napkins appear on tables during a communal meal in La Ceiba Garden & Kitchen at Rosewood Mayakoba. “Bien contentas,” said Chan Tuz, when asked how her neighbors have responded to the project. Samaranch explained: “It gives the women some independence. They have money and can manage their time. It’s something positive and very helpful, a job they can combine with what they do at home. Normally, they have to ask permission to work with us, but in this case, the men are grateful the women can contribute.”

Each worker gets to take home a basket of produce from the milpa as part of their wages. With only modest tiendas that stock junk food and shelf-stable canned goods, it’s generally a struggle to put fresh, healthy food on the table. (Especially when backyard milpas go untended because breadwinners are absent.) “We thought the people who grow the food should eat the food,” said Samaranch. “They get the same as the resorts we supply, so we have changed the diet.” He explained that children in San Pedro Chenchelá and the neighboring village of Kunché are now more excited about vegetables than soda or chips. “When a kid asks, ‘When will the eggplants be ready again?’ I feel we’re doing right.”

#6556. Blue whales have gone missing off the Galápagos. Scientists think El Niño could be why.
