#6492. NYC’s Hottest New Wine Bar Started With a DM Slide

An interview with the team behind El Camarón Peludo.

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar spent the last five years slinging tacos at breakneck pace to keep up with the lines at Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez and rowdy World Cup crowds at Socceria. Now the duo is slowing things down a bit for their first full-service restaurant El Camarón Peludo, a playful wine and seafood spot in the West Village where guests linger over mariscos.

At the tiny, walk-in-only restaurant, the menu fuses Mexican seafood dishes with Spanish influences and excellent wine from around the world. For the project, Cervantes and Apolinar teamed up with chef Carlos Barrera, a Mexico City-born chef who has worked in Michelin-starred restaurants in Spain and hosted dozens of popular pop-ups around NYC. When I sat down with Cervantes and Apolinar, I planned to pick their brains about how and why they manage four wildly popular (and very different) New York City restaurants. Then I learned how much El Camarón Peludo was the result of fate: If it weren’t for space constraints, a tapas-fueled trip, and a social media superfan, the duo may have had an entirely different restaurant on their hands.

Pre Shift: Where did the idea for El Camarón Peludo come from?

Tania Apolinar: When we were looking at [the space], we considered making it a taqueria, but because of the [long shape of the restaurant], it wouldn’t have worked for that concept. We knew we wanted to do something different, focused on seafood and wine.

Giovanni Cervantes: I was in conversation with Carlos about this idea to serve mariscos in New York when we saw the space. We didn’t know [at the time], but we were setting up the basis of the menu because we were talking about what we like and what we miss a lot [from Mexico]. We also talked about [our past trips] to Europe. We were really interested in how to match [the style of European tapas and wine bars] with what we do, which is the Mexican approach.

How did you connect with Barrera for the project?

Cervantes: Carlos was one of the first clients that we ever had in Taqueria Ramírez. We met basically through that and through Instagram. He was always commenting a lot...

Cervantes: Exactly. Sending the flame emoji. Then soon enough, we find out that we were neighbors because he lives in Greenpoint, so we started seeing each other more often.

Apolinar: Then we did a pop-up with him serving his famous Trompo Negro, which is like al pastor with [a smoky black spice paste that is widely used in Yucatán and surrounding regions], and that was the first time we actually connected in a working setup. We’re really aligned and happy with the partnership.

Can you tell me about how you balance Mexican and Spanish influences on the menu?

Cervantes: When we found the space, we knew it was the perfect setup to try something different. Then we made a trip to Europe and a trip to Mexico. After we came back from Europe, I think I was feeling very “Europeanized.” I remember having a conversation with Tanya and Carlos about making it even more Spanish, and both of them were like, “What?” And I’m glad they [pushed back], because we definitely found the right balance.

Apolinar: We’re talking about Mexican and Spanish, but in the end, it’s about the seafood and the freshness, the product that we really want to stand out. That’s why [we serve a] very simple gambas a la plancha, and the carpaccio has that approach as well, but then other more Mexican classics [like tostadas topped with tuna or aguachile] have more sauces and all of that.

Cervantes: And it’s not just the food. The influence that we took from different parts of Europe is the setup, the vibe, the size of the plates, the type of space. We want the space to feel cozy and friendly.

How is the service different from your other spots?

Cervantes: At Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez, it’s all about efficiency. Making it right, as fast as you can, and getting people in and out of the place. It’s nonstop volume. The consistency is awesome over there, and that’s [how we] measure that we’re making it right. Here it’s different. It’s more about the experience of the space and the music and the wine. [Our staff are] with these people for an hour or two, so you try to make it personal in a way. It feels different when you have that much time to see how people are enjoying the experience and transporting people to that world through what we’re doing. That’s comforting to me.

Now that you have four different restaurants around the city, how do you balance your time between them?

Cervantes: For Taqueria Ramírez, the very first one, we can sleep very well because almost everybody on the staff has been there since we opened. I’m just mentioning that because it’s all about building the right team because you can only be in one place at a time. Then at Carnitas, our partners [Yvon de Tassigny and Kari Boden] are really great and the plan was for them to be the day to day operators from the beginning. So right now we’re between El Cameron Peludo and Socceria because they’re the new babies and there’s a lot of work to do there.

Tania: It’s tiring, but at the end of the day, I’ve been enjoying it a lot. It’s nonstop but it feels rewarding to see the point of view of customers and make people feel happy and connect to them.

#6491. The Secret to Your Quarterback’s Arm Isn’t Just Luck or Athleticism. It’s Physics, Expert Explains.

A physicist breaks down the mechanisms of a perfect pass. You’ll never watch a game the same way.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

It’s Sunday afternoon on September 27. The play clock is winding down. San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy takes the snap and looks downfield. Receiver Mike Evans breaks toward the end zone, but the Cardinals’ defenders are closing in. Purdy releases the ball. It arcs above the turf, drops into the receiver’s hands, and the crowd roars. How did this seemingly perfect pass come together? Along with skill and strength, some fascinating science was at work.

Crucially, the quarterback needs to identify his intended receiver and get the football to the right location at exactly the right time. This split-second decision requires an implicit understanding of several important principles of physics, including projectile motion, speed, launch angle, angular momentum, and air resistance. Put this all together, and you might just clinch a seamless play.

As a physics lecturer at Clemson University in South Carolina, I spend my days analyzing the science that makes your favorite sports possible. For instance, in my Physics of Sports course, we seek to break down anything from ski jumping to boxing to pole vaulting, and this analysis is a sample of what that process might look like. Understanding these nuances completely reshapes how students watch games—and perhaps it will do the same for you.

Let’s start with some assumptions so we can cover the basics without additional variables: We will ignore air resistance for now and assume the quarterback and receiver will contact the ball at the same height. Once the football leaves the quarterback’s hand, it continues moving in the same direction because of its inertia, or the tendency of a moving object to stay in motion until a force changes its motion. Without gravity, the ball would continue moving in that upward direction forever. However, gravity pulls the ball downward as it flies, causing it to gradually slow on its upward trajectory. Eventually the ball reaches its highest point, the upward motion momentarily stops, and the ball accelerates as it falls back toward Earth.

The ball’s horizontal motion is very different because it maintains the same speed as it travels parallel to the field. Together, these vertical and horizontal motions create the ball’s familiar curved path, a parabolic trajectory. The shape of the trajectory depends on the speed and angle with which the quarterback throws the ball.

You might think that, to have the ball travel farther downfield, a player must throw it faster. However, it’s the trajectory that is key.

A low-angle throw (around 15 to 20 degrees) follows a relatively flat trajectory and therefore reaches the receiver quickly, though this enables defenders to intercept, because the ball travels close to the field. Alternatively, the quarterback can release the football at a higher angle (such as a throw at 50 degrees), producing a more pronounced arc. A greater launch angle allows the ball to travel above the reach of opposing defenders for much of its flight; however, it may not make the ball travel any farther downfield because more of its initial speed is directed upward and less is directed forward.

The trade-off in launch angle choice is that with greater throwing angles, more of the ball’s initial speed is directed upward rather than horizontally, increasing the time the ball spends in the air. While this can help the quarterback throw over defenders, it also gives both teams more time to react.

An interesting quirk of projectile motion is that complementary launch angles—two angles that add up to 90 degrees—produce the same horizontal range, provided the initial speeds are identical. For example, a football thrown at 30 degrees and one thrown at 60 degrees will travel the same distance downfield. However, the 60-degree throw will rise higher and remain in the air considerably longer. If the quarterback wants to maximize the distance of a throw, pitching the ball at a 45-degree angle produces the greatest horizontal range, because it balances the ball’s forward and upward motion to maximize its time in the air and its downfield travel.

Quarterbacks practice throwing balls with speed, which they can couple with a low launch angle to create a bullet pass. This type of pass travels low to the ground and the reception is completed very quickly, with the advantage that the opposition has very little time to reach the ball. To throw a ball as far as possible, the quarterback would choose to throw the ball as fast as possible at that aforementioned 45-degree angle.

So far, we know the quarterback can control the speed and angle of the pass—but that precision is all for naught if the ball isn’t heading toward someone who can catch it. In other words, the quarterback must be able to adjust these variables to make sure the football arrives in the right place at the right time.

Let’s imagine a receiver running a route that requires him to sprint downfield, change direction, and then break toward the sideline. The quarterback must anticipate how long it will take the receiver to reach the intended catching location. This depends on several factors, including the receiver’s running speed, route length, and any defensive traffic that might slow him down.

Knowing approximately how many seconds it will take the receiver to reach the anticipated location, the quarterback selects a throwing speed and an angle that delivers the football at that same moment. The quarterback is solving a timing problem: The motion of the football and the motion of the receiver must intersect at the same location at the same time. Spacecraft mission planners solve a similar issue when they chart where the moon will be when a spacecraft arrives, ensuring the two reach the same place simultaneously.

Experienced quarterbacks often throw before the receiver reaches the intended spot. After years of practice, they’re able to anticipate where the receiver will be when the ball arrives, rather than aiming at the receiver’s current position. If the timing is off, fans often gripe: “He just threw it away!”

As if controlling the speed, angle, and timing of a pass weren’t challenging enough, the quarterback also controls how the football rotates during flight. When a quarterback throws the ball well, it spins around its long axis, from point to point, stabilizing the football as it flies.

The physics principle behind this stability is conservation of angular momentum. A spinning football tends to resist changes to the orientation of its axis of rotation, which helps to prevent excessive wobbling during flight. This is the same basic principle that causes a spinning top to remain upright. When the top is spinning rapidly, it resists tipping over. However, as it slows down, the top becomes less stable and eventually begins to wobble and fall.

A football behaves similarly. Its spin helps maintain a stable orientation, allowing it to move through the air more efficiently. Although up to this point we have disregarded air resistance, aerodynamic forces do influence the ball’s orientation. Without sufficient spin, the football may tumble or wobble, increasing aerodynamic drag and making its flight less predictable.

Games don’t happen in a vacuum. Everything we’ve discussed thus far becomes even more complicated when we account for real-world conditions. On an actual football field, wind and air resistance—or drag—can significantly influence the ball’s motion.

If the quarterback is throwing into a headwind, the football experiences air resistance, which slows its forward motion because the oncoming air exerts a drag force opposite the ball’s motion through the air. To compensate, the quarterback may need to increase the throwing speed or adjust the launch angle to ensure that the ball reaches the intended receiver. On the flip side, if the wind is blowing in the same direction as the pass, it may help the football travel farther, requiring the quarterback to use slightly less throwing speed.

A crosswind creates another challenge. Wind blowing from the side can push the football away from its intended path. The quarterback may need to aim slightly upwind so that the football drifts toward the desired catching location.

Sudden gusts of wind are particularly difficult because they can change the football’s trajectory after it has already left the quarterback’s hand. He can no longer make corrections, and the ball may end up off course.

A quarterback’s throw depends on more than arm strength. The quarterback must judge the ball’s speed and direction, choose a launch angle, and account for the receiver’s movement and the ball’s spin, all while adjusting for environmental conditions. Then the quarterback must bring those decisions together in a controlled throw. Although quarterbacks don’t consciously solve projectile motion equations during a game, years of practice allow them to develop an intuitive understanding of these relationships.

In terms of a game, this might look like the following: Brock Purdy throws a beautiful spiral downfield, Mike Evans races toward the predetermined spot, and the quarterback’s prediction becomes a catch! The result may look effortless, but physics is at work from release to reception—and now you’ll never watch a game the same way again.

#6490. Students Test Prototype Landing Pad to Make Lunar Operations Safe

When spacecraft perform vertical landing and takeoff maneuvers from the lunar surface, the results are very messy! Beyond the intense heat produced by the rocket engines, the force also kicks up regolith, the particulate dust that covers most of the lunar surface. With so many crewed and cargo missions planned for the coming years, space agencies are contracting with commercial partners to develop infrastructure that will keep spacecraft, astronauts, and other surface elements safe from all "moondust."

This includes landing pads that provide a stable surface and barrier for vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) vehicles. To help them realize their objectives under the Artemis Program, NASA has enlisted engineers from the University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH) to create some. Their work is part of a multi-year partnership with Linc Research Inc., a certified engineering company located in Huntsville, Alabama, and supported through NASA's Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) program.

The student research team is led by Dr. Judy Schneider, a professor in UAH's Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering. Their research is focused on developing a design for modular, vented landing pads that will allow for safe transits to and from the lunar surface. This summer, the team successfully conducted three rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype of their landing pad at the university's Propulsion Research Center, demonstrating its ability to capture and redirect rocket exhaust through an integrated vent system.

Rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype lunar landing pad at the UAH Propulsion Research Center. Credit: Cadis Ammons

On Earth, landing pads consist of a solid structure capable of withstanding the full force and heat of a rocket plume. This can result in significant damage to the pad itself, as demonstrated by the first launch attempt of SpaceX's Starship prototype, including cratering beneath the mounting structure and sending debris flying in all directions. In contrast, the UAH team's design uses interlocking components with channels that help reduce thermal damage and protect the structure as well as the spacecraft.

For the tests, the team created individual concrete components and arranged them into a prototype measuring 3.65 m (12 ft) in diameter. The concrete serves as an analog for building materials that could be produced from lunar regolith, either "sintered" to form 3D-printed ceramics or combined with a bonding agent to produce "lunacrete." The components also had integrated sensors to record how the rocket plume's exhaust was channeled through the vent systems during the three firings.

The modular design also makes it easier to build on the Moon, where manufacturing centers are likely to be space-constrained. Smaller, individual components also mean future landing pads will be easier to assemble, expand, maintain, and repair over time. Combined with the use of local resources for building materials - aka. In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) - the team's goal could help make large-scale lunar infrastructure more feasible.

Earth's fluffy, dense atmosphere also helps prevent rocket exhaust plumes from expanding freely and kicking up dust. Because its only natural satellite is an airless body, dust clouds caused by impacts or rockets can travel all the way to the other side of the Moon. As a result, powerful blasts during takeoff and landing can propel dust at high speeds, potentially damaging nearby habitats, power elements, equipment, and other infrastructure. The dust can also be thrown into orbit, where it could interfere with orbiting satellites, space stations, and incoming spacecraft.

This marks a major step in developing landing infrastructure that will enable a lunar base and crewed operations in the near future. As Schneider said in a UHA press release:

On Earth, we use water-cooled flame buckets to redirect rocket exhaust. But we won't have those resources on the lunar surface, where water will be in limited supply. Our goal is to redirect the rocket plume so it doesn't damage the landing vehicle or any surrounding structures. The hot-fire tests demonstrated that we could redirect the rocket plume. By using an internally vented structure, we were able to prevent the heat from damaging the pad as it could in a solid structure.

With the initial tests complete, the team is now working on a 6 m-diameter (20 ft) landing pad that will be delivered to NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center (also in Huntsville) for additional testing and evaluation. These tests will further assess the design, push its technological readiness, and determine if the vented, modular approach can be scaled and adapted for repeated use. These efforts will bring the technology another step towards realization and deployment on the Moon.

Further Reading: University of Alabama Huntsville

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. #6489. Beyond the Iconic Potato Dish at New NYC Restaurant Somssi

There’s plenty of creative dishes coming out of this West Village kitchen

You’ve probably heard of the Potato Potato Potato dish at Somssi, the newest restaurant from Na:eun Hospitality. The triple-layered potato dish is the most labor-intensive dish on the menu but has also become the most popular order, with the kitchen going through up to 100 pounds of potatoes each week. The whimsical, caviar-topped dish really encapsulates what the restaurant is trying to achieve: “We should have serious food, serious hospitality, but we shouldn’t take ourselves too seriously,” says managing partner Ahris Kim. Here’s how the Somssi kitchen preps to create the newly famous potato and plenty of other dishes before a night of service.

Yukon gold potatoes are put through a ricer to become a cream and butter-heavy puree that is set in molds in the freezer. After being toasted in breadcrumbs, the logs of potato are wrapped in russet potato ribbons before being fried up to order.

Next is the ox tongue, which is brined for just over 16 hours before being slow-cooked in herbs, aromatics, and beef tallow for four hours. Huge cuts of tongue are carefully scored so they will get a great sear when they hit the grill. It’s served on a romesco sauce with just a bit of wasabi on the side.

Finally, pork loin is coated in ground shrimp for a creative schnitzel that is reminiscent of shrimp toast. The schnitzel is topped with a sweet-and-sour plum sauce that balances out the thick, crispy fried exterior. Scallop crudo is made up of pressed scallops surrounded with a strawberry sauce and topped off with gooseberries and peppers.

Watch the team at Somssi create creative dishes like a triple-potato bite and a show-stopping grilled tongue dish in this episode of Mise En Place.

#6488. My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them.

By all logic I should be sick of this chicken. I have cooked it, give or take, a hundred times. When I don’t know what to make for dinner—or, honestly, don’t want to make dinner at all—it is there for me, like a gentle friend.

The marinade is deceptively simple: equal parts miso and honey, plus a glug of soy sauce. Nothing more. There’s no gotcha moment, no pepper hiding in plain sight or olive oil I forgot to account for. The flavor excels because each ingredient punches above its weight. Both fermented, the miso and soy sauce add umami depth, while honey supplies sweetness and makes the chicken glossy, like ceramics pulled straight from the kiln.

I’m often deflated when I see the word marinade in a recipe. No, I don’t have time for “at least an hour” or, more likely, the dreaded “preferably overnight.” Don’t they know it’s a Tuesday? This marinade, mercifully, is immediate. Because it is more of a paste than a liquid, you can slather it directly onto the chicken before hurling the baking sheet into the oven. (Of course, if you’re the type of person who has the wherewithal to start meal prep the night before, that works too.)

A short stint under the fierce heat of the broiler transforms the miso coating into a burnished, sticky crust in 15-ish minutes while you work on the rest of the meal. Old-school drawer-style broilers can get a little overexcited, so start peeking in after 10 minutes. Now is not the time to check the mail or start a load of laundry.

This chicken shines with rice tucked underneath, which catches every saucy streak. But you could build it out with roasted vegetables. Sometimes I’ll add oiled-up broccoli or asparagus to the baking sheet. Other times it’s just the chicken, with a shower of scallions if I’m feeling fancy. Then I make it all again next week.

#6487. A Virtual Lifeless Earth Will Help Scientists Find Life on Exoplanets

In the search for life elsewhere in the galaxy, astronomers sift through exoplanet discoveries looking for ones that could be habitable. That means rocky planets with atmospheres in habitable zones. But one thing stymies these efforts. Can we examine atmospheres and differentiate between an exoplanet that's habitable and one that's actually inhabited?

That's difficult, partly because exoplanets are so far away, and also because we only have Earth to guide us. It's the only habitable and inhabited world we know of. But new research shows how we can work with those facts to try to detect inhabited worlds.

The work is "A Whole-planet Model of the Earth without Life for Terrestrial Exoplanet Studies," and it's published in The Planetary Science Journal. The lead author is Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, who was a postdoctoral astronomy student at the University of Washington when conducting this work.

"As the only known habitable (and inhabited) planet in the Universe, Earth informs our search for life elsewhere," the authors write. "Future telescopes like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will soon look for life on rocky worlds around Sun-like stars, so it is critical that we understand how to distinguish habitable planets from inhabited planets."

Observatories like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will inject new energy into the search for life. They will shift exoplanet science from identifying worlds that could be habitable, to identifying worlds with atmospheres showing signs of life. But as the researchers point out, we still don't know how to tell inhabited worlds, if there are any, from those that are merely habitable.

"Earth is currently the only known inhabited planet in the Universe, and geological evidence suggests that it was habitable with liquid-water oceans for most of its 4.54 Gyr history," the authors write. "Owing to its long-term habitability, Earth serves as the template that guides our search for biospheres elsewhere."

The researchers tackled this issue by building a sort of virtual Earth, but one without life.

"As a first step toward answering these questions, we present a coupled interior-atmosphere evolution model of the Earth without life from 50 Myr to 5 Gyr that reproduces 19 key observations of the preindustrial Earth after 4.5 Gyr within estimated measurement uncertainties," the researchers explain. Those 19 observations included atmospheric CO2 and H2O, surface temperature and albedo, ocean mass, and even factors like upper-mantle temperature and upper-mantle heat flow. These non-biological factors all shape a planet's atmosphere and have to be accounted for.

"Though exoplanet interiors themselves will likely never be directly observable, the effects of interior evolution are apparent in the composition of the atmosphere and the albedo of the surface environment, both of which HWO will observe on Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars via reflected-light spectroscopy," the authors explain.

This schematic shows some of the key processes included in the abiotic Earth model. Remotely observable quantities (surface temperature, albedo, and atmospheric H2O and CO2) are in bold. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

The researchers also produced reflected light spectra of the model Earth that covers the likely wavelength range of the HWO. They used a code to compute a "synthetic HWO reflected-light spectra (0.2â2.0 Î¼m) for the true Earth and the abiotic Earthâs atmospheric state after 4.5 Gyr," the authors write. These included line absorptions for CO2, H2O, O2, O3, and CH4.

This virtual Earth without life can serve as a benchmark to compare with detailed atmosphere observations of habitable worlds.

âThis model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets,â lead author Gilbert-Janizek said. "When we interpret observations of an exoplanetâs atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface.â

This schematic shows the atmospheric sources and sinks that define the new volatile cycling processes in the model. Fluxes related to CO2 are color-coded magenta, and fluxes related to H2O are color-coded teal. The schematic doesn't include ocean chemistry. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

Gilbert-Janizek didn't start from scratch. Senior author Rory Barnes, a UW associate professor of astronomy, had already built a model that included the core, mantle, crust and stellar radiation. This work added the surface and the atmosphere to build a more comprehensive model.

The authors hope that this model can serve as a kind of plug-and-play model that can be adjusted to fit with any particular exoplanet being studied. They can input factors like albedo and atmospheric CO2 and test what happens. If the model then recreates the observations of the planet, it suggests that the exoplanet in question is uninhabited.

Naturally, an undertaking of this size and complexity requires some assumptions. The model initializes after Earth's magma ocean solidified, and that dictated the atmosphere's initial composition. The authors say they chose an initial set of conditions "that apply after the bulk of the mantle has solidified."

They also assumed that plate tectonics were active during all of Earth's history beginning in the middle Hadean, which is widely believed to be true and in line with evidence. There are alternative hypotheses saying that this wasn't the case. One says that plate tectonics only began when it shifted from a stagnant-lid to modern plate tectonics during the Archaean, but the researchers avoided that.

Other assumptions were made regarding atmospheric pressure, the strength of Earth's geodynamo, and even atmospheric escape of hydrogen. But these types of assumptions are a normal part of science and are explained up front.

But the virtual Earth model successfully reproduces the properties of the Pre-Industrial Earth, and that's the most important thing. It also predicts that a planet can maintain habitable conditions for a long time without requiring the presence of life. This is relevant because false positives are one of the HWO's challenges.

These are three Engineering Architecture Concepts (EACs) for the Habitable Worlds Observatory. Each one features a different mirror design. EAC-1 is a 6m, segmented, off-axis telescope. EAC-2 is the same but uses a round keystone mirror and surrounding segments. EAC-3 is an 8m on-axis telescope with round segments. Not shown is the extendable, protective barrel that each design has, which will protect the mirror from micrometeorites. Image Credit: NASA Goddard/Conceptual Image Labs

âDr. Gilbert-Janizekâs work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,â Barnes said. âAfter more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr. Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earthâs core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate.â

The question "Are we alone in the Universe" can be asked in one breath but not answered in one. It has to be broken down to much smaller questions asked and answered across many generations. Even "Are we alone in the Milky Way" is far too large and encompassing a question. "Are we alone" has to be asked exoplanet by exoplanet, and that requires tools of the sort developed by Dr. Gilbert-Janizek and her colleagues.

Our first 6,000 exoplanet discoveries were bulk discoveries. But the search is becoming more targeted toward Earth-like planets, meaning tools like this one are becoming more and more necessary. The upcoming HWO, if it gets built, places this point in even finer focus.

âRealizing the ambitious goals of a telescope like the Habitable Worlds Observatory requires decades of work across many generations of scientists,â Gilbert-Janizek said. âIâm so grateful to join this lineage and one day pass the torch to the next generation so that we can continue chipping away at this question of whether or not we are alone in the universe.â

#6486. How Flavored Syrup Became a Coffee-Shop Culture War

For some coffee shop customers, premade syrups are now a major red flag. It presents a new opportunity for small business owners.

In a TikTok video with over 82,000 likes, the person behind the camera zooms into the shelves at a Pennsylvania coffee shop, three rows stacked with an array of Torani syrups in flavors like blueberry, brown-sugar cinnamon, English toffee, and salted caramel. “I just know my latte isn’t going to be good,” the caption reads. Across social media, similar sentiments appear. “If I see these at a cafe, I’m walking out immediately,” says one tweet, co-signed by many commenters. In a multipart video series, another creator documents her journey of replacing all of her Torani syrups with ones from small businesses instead. Last year, the niche food newsletter Unsnackable published what was described as a “Torani tirade.”

It’s not just a Torani problem, though the brand — by virtue of its market dominance — tends to get the most flack on social media. While some people seem to prefer competitor Monin, it, too, draws backlash over allegations of tasting “like chemicals.” The problem, for some drinkers of dessert-like specialty beverages, is premade syrups across the board.

For a certain sect of consumers, they’ve become a coffee shop red flag, a sign that a so-called “specialty” establishment asking them to fork over $8 plus tip for a latte is unfairly cutting corners when it comes to quality or craft. For these consumers, mass-market syrups now symbolize exactly that: They’re synonymous with coffee chains and corporations, the kind of impersonal institutions that many people are trying to get away from when they patronize a small business. The flip side: For independently owned coffee shops across the country, house-made syrup now represents a major opportunity.

When Carrie and Dennis Medina first envisioned their coffee shop, Room Service, in Ventura, California, they thought they would take an approach similar to the one at Sightglass Coffee, where they’d both gotten their start. “Very purist, with no syrups, no specialty drinks,” Dennis says. They imagined eight kinds of pour-over coffee and an emphasis on single-origin beans, since the couple also runs a roastery. “We said we’re never gonna do cream tops; we’re never gonna do these crazy drinks,” Carrie says. But in the first week alone, every customer was asking for them.

Now, Room Service offers 10 to 12 different syrups at any given time (and six different cream tops), all of them made in-house. It offers drinks such as a cinnamon roll latte topped with a cinnamon roll, and a honey cornbread latte with an ube cream top. “I hear that question all the time,” Dennis says. “‘Hey, do you guys make your syrups in-house?’” To him, a shop that isn’t trying to do at least the basics — like vanilla — in-house is “falling behind what the times are pushing for.”

The demand for syrups and other embellishments is so intense that the Medinas have brought on a full-time prep person who works exclusively on “all these things that we do in-house that make us special,” Carrie says. Room Service’s PSL, for example, starts with kabocha squash. It’s roasted, blended with spices such as cloves and cinnamon, and cooked into syrup, a process that takes two days. Echoing a sentiment that seems common among coffee shop owners right now, Carrie describes their current approach as “not necessarily the coffee shop we wanted, but it’s more like the coffee shop we have to be.” And if the market demands syrups and cream tops, then the Medinas wanted to ensure that the intention and emphasis on quality that they applied to their coffee beans also carried over.

In 2025, Michael Smith opened Trust Coffee Co. in Bay Village, Ohio, taking over, remodeling, and rebranding an older coffee shop. He, like the Medinas, imagined a more “pour-over, third-wave” style establishment. “But I’ve been a business owner for a long time,” says Smith, who also runs a restaurant and a catering business. “I’ve realized over the years that your customers tell you more about who you are than who you actually think you are.” His customers, it turned out, wanted seasonal syrups in niche flavors like maple rosemary, caramelized banana, and strawberry rhubarb.

The purist is no longer coffee’s north star; the maximalist is.

Syrups like Monin, which the shop’s previous iteration used, “serve a purpose in the industry,” Smith says, but he wanted more control over the menu. The two full-time pastry chefs from Smith’s other businesses oversee the shop’s syrups. “It’s become such a huge thing,” he says: Every time Trust’s social media manager posts a new syrup, the line is out the door for a week. “It sets us apart,” he explains.

When Sabrina Kaylor opened the first location of Bizarre Coffee in Canton, Georgia in 2020, the shop used bottled syrups. She hadn’t worked in coffee prior, and she said that approach felt like the norm at the time. “It allowed us to hone our craft and learn what we were doing,” she says. Over time, Kaylor — who’s quite active on the company’s official social media platforms — noticed that the tenor of the conversation was changing: In the immediate post-COVID years, people were making more things at home and there was more pride to be gained in “scratch-made.” With her business becoming known for lattes in flavors such as blueberry, banana, and guava, Kaylor decided to shift toward more house-made syrups. Previously, her customers didn’t ask about their sourcing, but now, they ask all the time.

As much as there is a sense of valor in the entirely from-scratch approach, Kaylor retains some skepticism about the current torrent of Torani and Monin backlash. Today, 90 percent of Bizarre’s drinks use house-made syrups, though one of its best-selling drinks still relies on the bottled stuff; Bizarre’s menu is extensive and making everything in-house would be a significant investment of labor. On the part of coffee shops, “I think a lot of [the house-made syrup conversation] is marketing, quite honestly,” Kaylor says. As for the bandwagoning that is all the anti-Torani memes, “I think it’s part of consumer behavior,” she says. And that, she acknowledges, can be really “discouraging” for small business owners.

In a sense, that’s what the premade-versus-house-made-syrup conversation boils down to: the stand between small businesses and big ones. For more consumers, the economic and social conditions of the current moment have inspired increased skepticism toward the influence of corporations and private equity in the food and beverage world.

The Minnesota coffee shop Little Joy has become famous across social media for posting the recipes of its signature drinks in detailed DIY videos. It has since launched a membership program through which other coffee shop owners can purchase its recipes, scaled up for commercial usage; gain access to training videos; and sell its drinks without even needing to attribute them to Little Joy, though the ones that would like to can pin their use of Little Joy’s recipes to a Drink Finder map.

Yes, these might just be recipes for syrups and foams, but in an interview with Eater’s industry newsletter Pre Shift earlier this year, Little Joy owner Cody Larson described the system as a way to build solidarity among independent businesses. “The big coffee chains, they’re never gonna do house-made syrups, so I think that’s where independent shops can get a leg up,” he said. “Ultimately, the chains are our competition... If independent shops can, in any way possible, raise the bar across the board, that’s good for all independent shops, including us.”

It’s hard to look at the drinks coming out of specialty coffee shops today — fluffy with foam, flavored to emulate nuanced desserts like princess cake and tiramisu— and not think of the Starbucks Frappuccino. The combination of app-ordering and social media “hack” culture have mainstreamed super-elaborate beverage requests, allowing Starbucks and coffee chains like it to become purveyors of highly complicated customizable beverages, mainstreaming the mindset of the aforementioned “hyperflavor.”

When it comes to why consumers have moved away from the single-origin pour-over approach at shops like his, “my guess is that these are a lot of people who used to be Starbucks loyalists and they’re looking for something that’s more local,” Smith says. “It’s a trend across everything where people want local, and we’re able to provide what Starbucks did, but in a more high-quality, more local way.”

Intentionality is what people are gravitating towards, especially as prices rise. If consumers are spending so much on a drink that’s undeniably a luxury, then they want to know that every part of that drink has been made carefully. And if they’re going to make the trip to a new, independent shop, they want to know that the offerings there aren’t the ones they can get anywhere, made with easily attainable, big-brand flavorings. For small coffee shops, the key to success could be as simple as syrup.

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6483. Giant Impacts Help Rocky Planets Retain Their Atmospheres

Earth's formation was a messy process. It all happened about 4.5 billion years ago, in our young chaotic Solar System. Rocky planetesimals were whizzing around in the Solar System back then, and Earth formed as more of these objects collided and merged with it.

Some of these collisions were giant impacts that generated immense heat. These were common in the later stages of Earth's formation, after the protoplanetary disk had largely dissipated and atmospheric accretion was complete. Planetary scientists have wondered how young planets like Earth could've held onto their atmospheres near the end of their accretion period. The massive heat from giant impacts should've driven primordial He/H atmospheres away. But new research suggests that simple picture doesn't capture some important details, and that giant impacts could've actually helped young rocky planets retain their atmospheres.

The work is titled "Retention of primordial atmospheres through giant impacts," and it's published in Nature Astronomy. The authors are Darius Modirrousta-Galian and Jun Korenaga. Modirrousta-Galian is a former Yale postdoc who is now at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Korenaga is a professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

This research focuses on what happens near the end of a rocky planet's accretion process, after the protoplanetary disk has largely dissipated. This is when other planetesimals had also grown large through their own accretion processes, and when they collided with a planet like Earth, they released an enormous amount of energy.

âGiant impacts are a key part of how rocky planets grow,â said co-author Korenaga. âPlanets the size of Earth or larger are expected to form through collisions between smaller planetary bodies. These collisions add mass and release enormous amounts of heat, which can drive atmospheric escape. Their effect on a planetâs atmosphere depends on how those two changes work together.â

Modirrousta-Galian and Korenaga have been working on how planetary interiors and atmospheres evolve together and have published several papers on the topic. Their previous research laid the foundation for this work.

Their work shows that increased heat near a planet's surface isn't the only result of impacts. Some of that heat is driven deep into the planet. The impact can also "increase atmospheric gravitational binding," according to the researchers.

There are two components of a giant impact: heat and mass.

This illustration shows planetesimals in a disk around a young star. Rocky planets grow by accretion of planetesimals, and as time goes on, the planetesimals become more massive. When these massive planetesimals impact young planets, they not only generate heat, they add mass. Image Credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech.

When a planetesimal smashes into a rocky planet, the heat can be divided into two separate components. Some of it is driven more deeply into the planet where it won't drive away the atmosphere. Some of it will be mantle heat that does contribute to driving the primordial atmosphere away. But the mass gained by the accretion of the planetesimal isn't divided. All of that mass gives the planet more power to hold onto its atmosphere.

"Whereas the entire accreted mass contributes to the increase in gravitational binding energy, only part of the impact energy raises mantle temperature," the authors explain. "Mantle melting consumes energy as latent heat, while the impactorâs metallic core transfers little energy to the mantle and remains superheated at depth."

"Giant impacts therefore increase gravitational binding energy more than mantle thermal energy, shifting planets towards atmospheric retention," the researchers explain.

This understanding can help explain the exoplanet population.

Astronomers used to think that our Solar System was an archetype of how other solar systems would look. There would be rocky planets in the inner Solar System, gas giants further out, and ice giants beyond them. But exoplanet discoveries have cast doubt on that. The most common types of detected exoplanets aren't even represented in our Solar System: super-Earths and sub-Neptunes.

Astronomers think that super-Earths and sub-Neptunes could represent two types of planets that started out as rocky cores but ended up with much different atmospheres. Super-Earths have lost their atmospheres, while sub-Neptunes have retained more of their primordial atmospheres. A sub-Neptune only needs to retain a few percent of its H/He atmosphere to have an extended puffy atmosphere that can increase its radius by a large amount.

These are artist's impressions of the super-Earth Kepler-452b (right) and the sub-Neptune Kepler-22b (left). They're very different from each other, and both types of exoplanet are abundant in exoplanet discoveries. Giant impacts could explain their abundance. Image Credit: NASA.

âWhy nature produces both types in such abundance is a fundamental puzzle in exoplanetary science,â said Modirrousta-Galian. âWe set out to find an explanation.â

This research shows that sub-Neptunes could have grown larger through more massive impacts, and those impacts not only added mass but allowed them to retain larger atmospheres. Super-Earth's weren't subjected to those same massive impacts, and so did not gain enough mass to retain their atmospheres the same way that sub-Neptunes did. They lost theirs due to stellar radiation.

This schematic shows different outcomes for rocky planets. In one scenario, massive impacts onto a rocky create a more massive planet that can retain more of its primordial atmosphere: a sub-Neptune. In the other scenario, there are no massive impacts, no increase in rocky mass, and the planet retains less of its atmosphere. Image Credit: Darius Modirrousta-Galian

"Larger, atmosphere-bearing planets emerge preferentially through collisional growth," the researchers explain. "By contrast, smaller planets without such impacts tend to lose their primordial atmospheres under sustained stellar irradiation. At the population level, these results suggest that sub-Neptunes have, on average, more massive rocky interiors than super-Earths."

These results appear to overturn the long-held idea that giant impacts spelled doom for planetary atmospheres, and in turn, for the prospects of habitability. Primordial H/He atmospheres themselves didnt create habitability. But some research shows that they're essential for the development of a world that is eventually habitable, through interactions with a young rocky planet's magma ocean. These interactions may have been a significant source of Earth's water and could be on other rocky worlds, too.

âThis overturns the decades-old canonical view that giant impacts almost always lead to complete atmospheric loss, demonstrating instead that these collisions can play a crucial role in the formation of sub-Neptunes,â Korenaga said.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Eater’s under-$25 holiday gift guide is, unabashedly, one of my favorites to curate during gift guide season — both as a shopping writer and a writer who lives, laughs, loves to shop. I live for the thrill of a thrifty find; that rush of finding the perfect gift that somehow comes in way under budget is a sensation I first experienced while thrifting with my mom as a kid, when I was taught to sniff out authentic English ironstone bowls like an Antiques Roadshow bloodhound. I have been John Wick-training for this moment.

The best gifts under $25 for the true food freaks in your life (including yourself) should speak to their specific culinary obsessions, tastebuds, and cult-fave restaurants. Keep an eye out for those limited-edition holiday gifts that are going to sell out soon, and, when you see a potential present, ask yourself: does it inspire whimsy? Why should I settle for a spoon rest that isn’t shaped like ravioli? Move those mugs and snacks from heritage and indie brands to the front of the line, and maybe even click add-to-cart twice so that you, too, can experience the magic of Spaghetti Dust.

Whether you’re looking for a White Elephant present or an offering to impress your in-laws, let’s shop for the best food- and drink-related gifts under $25.

Diaspora Spice Co. is one of my favorite places to buy spices online, because the selection is always exciting and the company pays its farm partners an average of six times more than the commodity price. This year’s enticingly versatile gingerbread spice blend caught my eye, because it can be used for baking, or for simply sprinkling over coffee for a festive boost. Bundle it up with a nice velvet bow and a highly specific, nostalgic thrift-store mug for a delightful gift.

The wonder elicited from this traveling tube of “Spaghetti Dust” — aka ready-to-sprinkle dried garlic, Calabrian chile flakes, parsley, and sea salt — with its groovy graphics and gift-ready packaging, makes it one of the coolest food-themed presents that’s sure to sell out this holiday season. Just add olive oil and al dente pasta, and you’re ready to eat a delicious meal.

There’s something so comforting about a stoneware mug — holding one makes me feel instantly more cozy and learned, like a Nancy Meyers character rediscovering joy in an English countryside cottage. The ceramic material makes stoneware a great insulator when it comes to heat retention (without burning your hands), and this rustic, splatter stoneware mug from Hudson Grace is a looker.

Your giftee has all the deep-cut Kewpie mayonnaise flavors. They might even own the Kewpie cookbook. Now, give them the gift of a Kewpie mayo ornament to solidify their fealty to the Japanese mayo brand.

Ya Albi is a Palestinian American, mother-daughter-owned company that sources its slightly sweet, full-bodied olive oil from the West Bank, and packages it all in a chic pink tin. Plus, all of the oil’s proceeds go toward HEAL Palestine, a nonprofit organization that supports Palestinian children impacted by the war on Gaza. (To shop for even more Palestinian olive oils, check out this Eater guide.)

Technically, it’s 20 cents over our $25 budget, but this princess cake-inspired soap from Flamingo Estate is too good to pass up. #6481. Less Sugar in Early Life Could Protect Your Mental Health Decades Later

An observational study links sugar rationing in early life to lower adult anxiety and depression risks, raising the possibility that our earliest diets have lasting mental health implications.

Could the amount of sugar we consume before birth and during infancy influence our mental health decades later? An experiment rooted in postwar Britain suggests that the effects of our earliest diets may extend far beyond childhood.

During World War II and the years that followed, the United Kingdom strictly rationed sugar, limiting how much families could purchase. When those restrictions ended in September 1953, sugar consumption surged, creating a rare opportunity for scientists to examine how early-life exposure to sugar might shape long-term health.

A study published in General Psychiatry found that exposure to rationing during early life was associated with a 17% lower risk of anxiety and a 14% lower risk of depression compared with no exposure. The researchers analyzed data from 66,223 UK Biobank participants born around the policy change, linking the timing of their earliest years to health records later in life.

Because the availability of other foods remained relatively stable when sugar consumption increased, the end of rationing offered a natural experiment. Researchers could compare people who experienced different periods of restricted sugar availability at the start of life. They estimated exposure using birth dates relative to the policy change, with exposure ranging from before birth only to periods extending through about age two.

That approach tracked exposure to a national policy, rather than measuring what individual mothers or children ate. The researchers did not have individual childhood food records, and unmeasured factors, including other aspects of maternal diet, may have influenced the results. The findings therefore cannot establish that lower sugar intake caused the differences in mental health.

The strongest associations appeared among people exposed to rationing throughout the first 1,000 days after conception, spanning pregnancy and roughly the first two years after birth. Compared with people without early exposure, this group had approximately 24% lower relative risk of anxiety and 21% lower relative risk of depression. Across the analysis, the association generally strengthened with longer exposure to rationing.

For participants exposed throughout those first 1,000 days, diagnoses also appeared later in their health records. The first recorded anxiety diagnosis occurred about two years later, and the first recorded depression diagnosis about four years later, than among participants with no early exposure. These findings concern when diagnoses were first recorded, rather than necessarily when symptoms began.

Early nutrition could potentially influence later mental health through its effects on stress regulation, inflammation, and brain development. The authors drew these possible explanations from previous research, but did not directly test the mechanisms in the UK Biobank analysis. Further studies that measure individual diets and examine other populations will help clarify how dietary conditions during pregnancy and infancy relate to mental health across the life course, and what that relationship could mean for public health.

Reference: “Sugar restriction during the first 1000 days after conception and its association with decreased risk of anxiety and depression” by Xiuping Dou, Yang Su, Yao Huang, Man He, Bingying Zhang, Xuejin Li, Hualiang Lin and Yin Yang, 7 July 2026, General Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1002/gps3.70038

The sale of the Nanotyrannus "Jodi" for over $47 million shines a stark light on the commodification of Earth's history. By selling dinosaurs off to the highest bidder, we lose what makes them valuable in the first place.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place.

On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024.

Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors.

There are three main reasons why. First: Fossils are evidence, not objects. A dinosaur's bones can reveal how it grew, moved, fed, and lived. They preserve traces of injury and disease, help reconstruct ancient ecosystems, and offer clues about the "rules of life" governing our world that scientists are still learning to interpret.

Jodi illustrates exactly why access to physical evidence matters. For nearly half a century, paleontologists debated whether Nanotyrannus was a distinct dinosaur or simply a juvenile T. rex. A lack of well-preserved fossils available for study only fueled the uncertainty. And then a remarkable specimen, once in private hands, moved into the public trust.

The fossil was uncovered in Montana in 2006 alongside a Triceratops. Dubbed the "Dueling Dinosaurs," it took until 2022, and an appeal in the state's Supreme Court, for the remains to be acquired by the Museum of Natural Sciences so they could be fully studied. This research provided a powerful new perspective, arguing that Nanotyrannus lancensis was a distinct dinosaur and, moreover, that a second species of Nanotyrannus once roamed the American West.

When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow.

This hypothesis has big implications for the health of ecosystems before one of Earth's most severe extinction events — but it currently rests on the scant few Nanotyrannus specimens housed in public collections. Specimens like Jodi could uphold or dethrone it. Without access, we, and Jodi’s true identity, will remain in the dark.

It is hard to overstate the irony of Jodi's sale: a specimen recently listed as a juvenile T. rex now captures the world's imagination, and commands double the price tag, as a "Nanotyrannus." Yet if a similar fate had befallen the Dueling Dinosaurs and they had remained in private hands, we would not have known for certain that Nanotyrannus ever existed.

Scientific progress depends on researchers being able to compare specimens, test hypotheses, and revisit earlier conclusions. When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow. This is why access to the evidence must endure.

This brings us to the second problem with privately owned dinosaurs. Digital scans cannot replace the original fossil.

Three-dimensional scans and digital models are powerful tools. We use them to measure bones, compare anatomy, share information, and educate the public. But digital models capture only the most superficial aspects of a fossil's story.

The auction took place on Oct. 27, with Jodi eventually selling for around five times the top estimate.

To understand dinosaur growth, we examine microscopic structures inside fossilized bone through a technique called bone histology. We also analyze the chemistry of fossils to investigate diet, migration patterns, and metabolism. Such work requires physical samples, not just images of a bone's surface. We also need contextual data about the surrounding sediments, preservation mode, and ancient environment in order to explore questions about the ecosystems in which the animals once lived. Much of this information is lost in the rush to excavate and prepare fossils as quickly as possible for the auction block. It can never be reclaimed.

We cannot predict what novel technologies future researchers will employ to make new discoveries from old bones, or even which questions they will ask. Technology will continue to advance, bringing analytical methods we cannot anticipate. A scan made today does not guarantee that researchers will have the physical evidence needed for tomorrow's discoveries. Digital access should complement preservation of original specimens, not justify losing it.

Finally, private ownership cannot guarantee lasting public access. Yes, some private collectors financially support research and education and donate specimens they purchase. Those contributions are valuable. But the issue is not whether an individual owner is generous; it is whether access is guaranteed over time.

A temporary loan is insufficient. A loaned specimen can be withdrawn, sold, or inherited by someone with different priorities, situations that are becoming increasingly common in the U.S. and abroad. By contrast, a fossil deposited in a responsible public research institution is documented, cared for, studied, and made available to future researchers and educators in perpetuity. The question is not whether people should be able to admire dinosaurs; it is whether the evidence that helps us understand them will remain available to everyone.

Nor should museums consider selling scientifically important fossils to cover operating shortfalls. Collections are not ordinary financial assets to liquidate when budgets tighten. Selling an irreplaceable specimen provides a one-time payment while sacrificing future scientific potential. Museums need sustainable funding for collections care, research, and education, not pressure to trade away the very resources they exist to preserve.

Jodi's sale is complete, but the fossil's long-term future remains uncertain. With the buyer's identity undisclosed, the public cannot know what arrangements, if any, will ensure continued access for researchers and educators. We hope the new owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education, through permanent placement in a public research institution. But hope is not a substitute for a guarantee.

There is a better way to support paleontology. Enthusiasts who want to share in the excitement of discovery can fund fieldwork and research, endow curatorial positions, strengthen museum collections, or donate important fossils to public institutions where we can all learn from them.

Dinosaurs inspire wonder because they connect us to a world vastly different from our own. But their importance extends far beyond their power to captivate us. They are part of our shared natural heritage and an irreplaceable record of Earth's history.

We should measure a dinosaur's worth not by the price it commands at auction, but by the knowledge it can help us build, and by whether we preserve that opportunity for generations to come. Earth's history belongs to all of us, not to the highest bidder.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Nov. 4 at 8.22 a.m. ET to correct the year the Museum of Natural Sciences acquired the Dueling Dinosaurs.

She is also an Associate Research Professor at NC State University, President of the Jurassic Foundation, and Chair of the Ethics Committee for the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology. Her work champions transparency, inclusivity, and public access to science.

#6478. Game Theory Helps SETI Search for Alien Civilizations

The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) is mostly concerned with where to look for technosignatures from another civilization. Between 2012 and 2015, SETI's Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 Sun-like stars for signs of Intelligent life. But where to look might not be as important as when to look, according to scientists at SETI.

In a new paper, scientists outline the effort to search for signals not only in the right place, but at the right time. The paper is "A Technosignature Survey Of The Anti-Solar Point: The SETI Institute's Largest-Ever Campaign With The Allen Telescope Array," and it was presented at the 77th International Astronautical Congress. The authors are Isabel Gerrard and Sofia Z. Sheikh. Gerrard is the Technosignature Researcher with Breakthrough Listen at the University of Oxford, and Sheikh is a SETI Institute Research Scientist.

âThe challenge in SETI isnât simply deciding where to point a telescope. Itâs figuring out where and when another civilization might choose to transmit." - Dr. Sofia Sheikh, SETI Institute Research Scientist.

The new search effort doesn't do away with the "where" aspect of the search. Since life exists around stars, this search is still focused on stars, or rather the planets that orbit them. But it's different this time. This time it involves a point changes over time, called the antisolar point. It's the point in space-time that's directly opposite from the Sun from the perspective of an observer.

Imagine a line extending from the Sun, through an observer on Earth, and out the other side. It's not fixed in place; it's an abstract point defined by changing coordinates that shifts as the Earth orbits the Sun.

This simple static illustration shows the antisolar point. (created with AI)

This new SETI effort is also inspired by game theory. Game theory is a way of anticipating another player's moves in a game, when their moves are also based on their anticipations of your next move. The most well-known example of game theory is probably the Prisoner's Dilemma. In this case, the other player is another intelligent civilization conducting their own SETI-like effort.

What it boils down to is trying to predict when and where we can detect a purposeful transmission from another civilization and send our own, and also when and where they're doing the same.

"We borrow from game theory the concept of Schelling points to hypothesize spacetime coordinates where both we and an extraterrestrial agent might send and search for a signal," the authors write. Schelling points are also called focal points in game theory. "From the perspective opposite the Sun, an extraterrestrial agent could detect Earth transiting within the habitable zone, thus this Anti-Solar Point (ASP) poses a shared and salient Schelling point."

Resources are limited, and the better we or an alien civilization can use them, the greater the chances of success. If they can figure out the most effective time and place to send a radio signal, they increase their chances of success. The same is true for us. There's a synergy in it.

"A Schelling point is a default solution two agents both naturally arrive at, without communication, because of some shared cultural understanding of prominence in the given context," the authors write. "The predictability of a Schelling point relies on a common understanding of the prominent features in this context, and the mutual awareness of each otherâs knowledge."

So without any prior communication, both we and another extraterrestrial agent would identify the same place to send and receive signals: the antisolar point. The choice is based on our shared understanding of astronomical transits, or what we call the transit method in the hunt for exoplanets. It's almost certain that another civilization would also use this method because it presents itself naturally.

"It follows that if an ETA (Extraterrestrial Agent) also used the transit method in their search for life, they would detect Earth against the Sun as habitable and classify Earth as an eligible target for interstellar communication," the researchers explain.

This simple animation shows how the antisolar point moves and how an exterrestrial observer would detect Earth's transit. (AI-generated)

At the midpoint of Earth's transit in front of the Sun, from the ETA's perspective, Earth would be directly between them and the Sun. "From the perspective opposite the Sun, once each year an extraterrestrial agent could detect Earth transiting within the habitable zone, thus this antisolar point poses a shared and salient time-coordinate Schelling point," the authors write.

The search using the Allen Telescope Array and the antisolar point is called the ATA-ASP survey. It's a multiyear effort, and its initial findings are already here. Because it's based on the ASP, the survey isn't constant, it's intermittent. As Earth orbits the Sun, the ASP keeps changing, and it takes several years to cover it.

One of the Allen Telescope Array's dishes. The ATA-ASP survey will be the ATA's largest survey effort, collecting 11 petabytes of data over four years. Image Credit: Photo taken by Isabel Gerrard and edited by Ananya Kalapatapu

"Provided that half of the ecliptic is inaccessible in a year (the portion that is daytime), the campaign requires at least two years of observing sessions to sample every possible ASP along the ecliptic," the authors explain. "Furthermore, due to the â¼ 365.25 day orbit of the Earth (inciting the leap day every 4 years), the accessible nighttime portion of the ecliptic slightly precesses in successive years, ergo total survey coverage requires staggering observations over the course of four years." For these reasons, the ATA isn't solely occupied with the ATA-ASP survey.

The first pilot results are from August August 30th, 2024 until August 25th, 2026. Obviously, ATA-ASP didn't detect any alien signals or we would've almost certainly heard about them already. But for SETI, the results mark a milestone. Searching the ASP for signals was first proposed decades ago, and now they've finally done it.

ATA-ASP detected an enormous number of radio signals, about 1.9 million in 17 hours of observations. But they were all from human sources. Those detections were still an important test of the system though.

As things stand now, the ATA-ASP campaign has gathered another 121 nights of observations since the initial pilot. Those results haven't been shared yet.

âThe challenge in SETI isnât simply deciding where to point a telescope,â said co-author Sheikh. âItâs figuring out where and when another civilization might choose to transmit. The anti-solar point gives us a way to think about that problem from the perspective of a potential sender, rather than just the receiver.â
