#6459. Asteroids' Oddball Shapes Make Deflecting Them Challenging

If you're looking for uniformity in Nature, you won't find it in the asteroid belt. Not only are asteroid compositions different because they come from different parent bodies, but their shapes are different, too. They're not massive enough to round themselves like planets do.

This is more than just another space factoid; asteroid shapes matter. It's a near-certainty, given enough time, that a dangerous asteroid will head directly for a collision with Earth, and that's something scientists are actively studying. They want to develop ways to knock an asteroid off course, if necessary. That's what NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and the ESA's follow-up Hera mission were about.

There are multiple concepts for redirecting a dangerous asteroid. One of them is a nuclear weapon. Not to obliterate an asteroid, but to bombard it with radiation by exploding the nuclear weapon in close proximity to the asteroid. This is called a stand-off X-ray mitigation scenario. The radiation pulse will change an asteroid's course, if done soon enough and done correctly.

But the outcome of the pulse needs to be predictable to work, and that's where asteroids' different shapes come into play.

"The effectiveness of deflecting Near Earth Objects (NEOs) using pulsed radiation is challenging to quantify because it hinges critically on surface topography, which is often unknown," write the authors of new research in Icarus. The research is "Efficient computation of vapor ejecta over asteroid geometries during pulsed energy deflection," and the lead author is Nathan Moore. Moore is a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories.

A simple kinetic impactor is probably the preferred choice for deflecting an asteroid. That's what the DART mission did, and it appeared to be successful. Though it only changed the velocity of its target Dimorphos by a little, it was done soon enough to create a substantial change in its position over years.

But the more pertinent issue concerns an asteroid, or perhaps a comet, that's on a collision course with Earth, but isn't discovered soon enough for an impactor to effectively change its trajectory.

"While considered an option of last resort, it has been argued that late-time interception of a near-Earth object (NEO) or comet, either for disruption or deflection, might only be possible with the higher energy concentration available from detonation of a pulsed energy device," the authors write. 'Pulsed energy device' is one way of saying nuclear weapon. In space, there's no atmospheric shock wave from a nuclear explosion, only radiation, which is released in a powerful pulse.

"Stand-off energy burstsâthose detonated far from the surfaceâhold a potential advantage compared to surface explosions in that they might permit deflection with less disruption to the original structure, allowing for more controlled steering of the asteroid and its debris," the authors write. Disrupting the original structure might make for a good action sequence in a movie, but it would multiply the hazard to Earth by creating a swarm of debris, some of which could strike our planet.

Researchers have simulated using nuclear weapons and their radiation pulses to deflect asteroids, but their irregular shapes have stymied them. These shapes are far more difficult to model, so most research has focused on spherical asteroids. Moore and his colleagues developed a new algorithm to overcome these limitations.

âOur new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough,â Moore said. âWith the old models, computers just couldnât handle it.â

In this research, the authors simulated known asteroids with more irregular shapes, an important improvement on previous work.

"The approach improves on earlier methods by accounting for the actual topography of the asteroid fully in three dimensions without unacceptably increasing computational cost or reducing accuracy," the authors explain. "As a demonstration, we predict the deflection of three bodies of different shapeâasteroid (101955) Bennu, asteroid (25143) Itokawa, and asteroid (6489) Golevkaâfrom both near-field and far-field irradiations."

These images of asteroids Itokawa (left) and Bennu (middle), and a computer model of asteroid Golevka (right), show how asteroid shapes can be very different from one another. Image Credits: Itokawa: By ESO, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=170826264. Bennu: By NASA/Goddard/University of Arizona - Public Domain. Golevka: By NASA/JPL - NASA - Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Public Domain.

A sequence of events unfolds after a nuclear device is detonated near an asteroid. First, an intense x-ray pulse is directed at one side of the asteroid. Then there's rapid surface vaporization, and that creates most of the deflection thrust. Next is an internal shock wave, a powerful blow that travels through the asteroid's body. Finally, the internal structure of the asteroid is fractured, and that can blow chunks of the asteroid off the surface opposite the blast, and off of the asteroid's sides.

So despite there being no atmospheric shock wave, the asteroid is still disrupted.

The results highlighted how important an asteroid's shape is. Depending on which side of the asteroid was facing the radiation blast, the deflection velocity can be up to five times greater. "We find that the orientation of the body at time of intercept can increase the deflection velocity by up to nearly 2Ã for Bennu, 4Ã for Itokawa, and 5Ã for Golevka, compared to the minimum response for each body," the authors write.

This figure shows the pressure distribution as averaged over the first 20 Î¼s of vapor expansion, for asteroid (a) Bennu, (b) Itokawa, and (c) Golevka, for near and far Height Of Bursts (HOB). The vaporization is what creates most of the deflection thrust. Image Credit: Moore et al. 2026. Icarus.

âWe expected aim to matter,â said lead author Moore in a press release. âWhat surprised us was how much.â

The simulation in this work can be used on any asteroid that's been mapped by a spacecraft during a flyby. The size of the explosion, the distance, and the surface exposed to it can all be calculated in advance. By calculating the surface vaporization, the main factor in deflection, the simulation determines how hard the asteroid will be pushed, how fast it will rotate, and how much of the surface might break up.

The interior structure of asteroids can be quite different, and that's beyond the capabilities of this model to account for. "Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We canât predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Real life is always different from simulations, and that means that these results can't tell us with absolute certainty what will happen. But it's a step forward, one that drives home how critical the aim is to a successful asteroid deflection, should one be needed in the future.

"The strong sensitivity of deflection and disruption to asteroid topography is especially pertinent given that the shape of an incoming NEO might not be known, and its orientation at time of intercept may be uncontrolled," the authors write. Their work as it stands now can at least be used to make estimates, which is better, far better, than nothing.

"Alternatively, effort could be made to obtain high-resolution topographic characterization of an incoming NEO to improve accuracy of the deflection model, such as using spacecraft-based imagery or altimetry acquired before detonation," the authors explain.

It's possible that asteroid-mapping spacecraft could stand at the ready in space, waiting to be deployed. They could even be paired with asteroid-disrupting spacecraft carrying nuclear weapons. Or the two capabilities could be combined into one spacecraft. Placing atomic weapons in space would be extremely tricky in our fractured geopolitical world, but it's still a possibility, maybe the only possibility.

But however we prepare for an incoming asteroid, this work highlights how important it is that our aim is true.

âOur study shows how important it is to aim carefully,â Moore said. âPick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.â

#6458. Scientists Reveal How a Mysterious Brain Structure Keeps Memories From Fading

Memories that last only seconds shape everyday thinking, and research in mice is revealing how a small brain structure supports an ability impaired in ADHD and schizophrenia.

To understand a sentence, the brain has to keep earlier words in mind as new ones arrive. Working memory makes that possible, holding information for a few seconds so we can compare it with new information, manipulate it, and use it to guide our behavior.

We rely on it to follow conversations, solve problems, and decide what to do next. Yet sensory information fades within moments once a stimulus ends, leaving the brain with the demanding task of maintaining a usable representation of something that is no longer there.

In mice, researchers at UNIGE have found that this ability relies partly on the claustrum, a thin structure deep within the brain between the insular cortex and the striatum. Their findings appear in Nature Communications.

The scientists tested mice on tasks that required them to remember either a smell or a touch. Each animal received an initial stimulus, waited several seconds, and then received a second stimulus. The mouse had to determine whether the two were identical or different. By the time the second stimulus arrived, the first was gone, so success depended on retaining information about it during the wait.

Temporarily reducing the activity of claustrum neurons cut the mice’s working memory performance in half. To control these neurons at precise moments during the task, the researchers used techniques including optogenetics. This method uses specific proteins to make selected neurons sensitive to light, allowing scientists to alter their activity through an optical fiber. The intervention helped establish that the claustrum contributes to working memory rather than simply becoming active while another brain region does the necessary work.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” says study co-leader Alan Carleton, Full Professor in the Department of Basic Neurosciences at UNIGE’s Faculty of Medicine. “Moreover, disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself.”

Working memory depends on interactions across a broad network that includes the prefrontal cortex, sensory regions, the parietal cortex, the thalamus, and other structures beneath the cortex. These networks must preserve information while allowing the brain to continue perceiving, thinking, and acting, but how they maintain a representation over time remains largely unknown. The claustrum’s anatomy offers a reason to examine its contribution.

“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” explains Carleton.

Recordings from the mice allowed the researchers to examine how information was represented in claustrum activity during the gap between stimuli.

“Our live recordings of claustrum neuron activity showed that a trace of the initial information persisted throughout the entire waiting period,” says fellow study leader Ivan Rodriguez, Full Professor in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE’s Faculty of Science. “Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time. Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”

“Our discovery could help us better understand cognitive disorders in which working memory is impaired, such as schizophrenia or ADHD,” explains Carleton. “Identifying the brain circuits that allow information to be maintained over time is an important step towards understanding how these functions can be disrupted. We now need to determine how the claustrum communicates with cortical networks, and how this interaction preserves the fidelity of the representations held in working memory.”

Reference: “The claustrum contributes to working memory maintenance in mice” by Anindya S. Bhattacharjee, Maxime Juventin, Chieko Huber, Burak Unsal, Jean-Rodolphe Renfer, Ivan Rodriguez and Alan Carleton, 14 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78363-6

Magma and a possible environment for ancient life might be present on Mars in the region of a large volcano on the Red Planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A noxious gas found seeping through cracks on Mars hints that there may be magma flowing beneath the Red Planet's surface — and perhaps even an environment similar to habitable ones on Earth, a new study suggests.

Europe's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) spacecraft spotted a possible signal of hydrogen chloride gas leaking from rifts in the region of Alba Mons, the largest volcano on Mars in terms of surface area. (Mars' famous Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in terms of height.) Scientists interpret this gas as emissions from hot magma below the regolith of Mars.

Although more research is required to confirm the emissions, the team suggested that Alba Mons may host an environment similar to hydrothermal vents on Earth, where life once likely arose and continues to thrive today.

The study, published in the journal Science Advances Wednesday (Nov. 4), is not the first to suggest that magma may be flowing on Mars; NASA's InSight lander interpreted its presence through seismic observations and modeling earlier this year. But the new findings are the strongest evidence yet of gases being released by dormant volcanoes on Mars, first study author Alexander Trokhimovskiy, at Russia's Space Research Institute, told Live Science.

"Our study offers a complementary and potentially independent line of evidence [of Martian magma]: Atmospheric observations that reveal a possible signature of gas release from a subsurface magmatic system," Trokhimovskiy wrote in an email.

TGO first detected hydrogen chloride gas in Mars' atmosphere in 2021, but scientists were hesitant to link it to volcanic activity. The gas appeared to be seasonal, its distribution was not localized at a possible volcanic region, and other signs of volcanic gases, like sulfur, were not present, study co-author Kevin Olsen, a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford who studies Mars gases, told Live Science in a separate email.

A photo of Mars with the Tharsis region centered.

Further work, however, suggested that the gas wasn't just popping up in the warmer spring and summer in Mars' southern hemisphere; it also appeared in the winter in the northern hemisphere, he noted.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"I managed to catch two observations from the start of northern winter in the first Mars year of our mission, and a single observation the next year," Olsen said, adding that a year on Mars is closer to two years on Earth due to the planet's wider orbit. "These out-of-season measurements were close to one another in location and time in both years, which was rather surprising. We then set about creating a campaign of special, targeted measurements at this time and place."

That campaign lasted two Mars years — roughly four Earth years — and increased the likelihood that scientists are seeing "an injection" of hydrogen chloride into the atmosphere from volcano-adjacent vents, Olsen said.

The scientists confirmed the unseasonal observations in the northern hemisphere, finding a "distinct and pronounced signal" that then diminishes and falls below the spacecraft's detection threshold. "This inconsistency is more suggestive of a puff of gas entering the atmosphere than of regular atmospheric chemistry," he said. "While the link remains a hypothesis, we have now seen this gas appear locally, and nowhere else, over four Mars years of observations."

Daniel Mège, also a co-author of the paper and a professor who studies planetary geology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, identified the fissures where the gas may be emerging. He said the complementary evidence from InSight (on the ground) and TGO (circling above) helps give the study weight: InSight spotted activity in the crust, while TGO detected the emissions in the atmosphere.

Although magma activity is not in itself a sign of life, Mège noted that Earth's first life-forms came from sites like hydrothermal zones, which have a similar confluence of materials and energy as the potential vents on Mars. But conditions would need to be favorable in that area for at least millions of years to allow life to form, he cautioned.

"If these requirements are met at local scale, at the scale of the seepage structures, then living organisms might wait for us to discover them," he told Live Science in an email. "But maintaining stable conditions over such a long period at a very local scale is not obvious."

#6456. 'Big Bang' Fix Puts Voyager Across the 'One Light-Day' Mark

An innovative solution helps to put the venerable Voyager 1 spacecraft past a key milestone.

Flashback to 1977. Jimmy Carter was U.S. president, Star Wars was a box office hit, and the two Voyager spacecraft departed on an historic Grand Tour of the solar system. Now, teams at NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory are working to keep the missions active, as they push the boundaries of interstellar space beyond the solar system.

NASA recently announced that after a brief bit of drama and loss of communications with Voyager 1, a fix dubbed the âBig Bangâ was successful in resuscitating the spacecraft. The Big Bang swap alternated three units (two primary heaters and an old 8-track digital tape recorder) with three low power secondary options. The brief loss of communications occurred on October 20th, and lasted for 48 hours.

Engineers work on a Voyager spacecraft prior to launch. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

âThis is the first time weâve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,â said Kareem Badaruddin, in a recent press release. âWeâre relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.â

The Big Bang method was also successfully implemented to keep Voyager 2 functioning this past August.

Traveling far from the Sun, the Voyager missions rely on Plutonium-fueled radioisotope thermoelectric generators for power. PU-238 has a half-life of just under 88 years, meaning the missions are now steadily losing power.

This loss equates to about 4 watts of power each year. Voyager 1 currently utilizes a little over 200 watts of power, about enough to power an electric blanket. This has forced mission controllers to make some tough choices, including turning off the Low Energy Charged Particle experiment LECP in early 2026. The missions launched with 10 instruments in 1977.

The swaps had to occur at the same time, as the units involved also heat the spacecraft and assure that it continues to operate in the chilly depths of deep space.

Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, actually after Voyager 2. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. A flyby past enigmatic Titan to get a close look on November 12, 1980 meant the mission would depart the plane of the solar system afterwards. Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989.

The paths of Voyagers 1 and 2 out of the solar system. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

The Voyagers continue to do science as they travel through interstellar space beyond the fringes of the outer solar system. The two Voyagers are the first missions to sample the region of space beyond the heliosphere directly.

The Voyagers head out beyond the bowshock of the solar system into interstellar space. Credit: NASA

Right now, the important Plasma Wave Subsystem (PWS) plus a magnetometer instrument on Voyager 1 remain active. Without the Big Bang shuffle, mission controllers would have had to make the hard decision turn off yet another crucial instrument in 2027.

Voyager 1 witnesses a 'crescent Saturn'. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Moving at 16.9 kilometers per second relative to the Sun and the solar system, Voyager 1 will become the first human-made artifact to reach the one light-day mark this month on Wednesday, November 18th at 5:16 AM EST. Thatâs roughly 26 billion kilometers or 172 Astronomical Units (AU) distant. For context, the Moon and cis-lunar space marking the farthest humans have traveled to date is just over one light-second distant.

NASAâs global Deep Space Network continues to monitor the ever fainter signals from the Voyager spacecraft. Controllers will likely have to contend with more signal outages in the years to come.

The worldwide DSN tracks missions including one of the Voyager spacecraft. Credit: NASA/DSN

Along with the now silent Pioneers 10 and 11 and the still active New Horizons mission, Voyagers 1 and 2 are now leaving the solar system for galactic space. The upper stage Star boosters that help these missions achieve escape velocity are on their way outbound as well. The next mission escaping the solar system wonât happen for a while, though the proposed Interstellar Probe mission could one day make the trip. Voyager 1 is now outbound in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus near its border with Hercules.

Congrats the intrepid and resourceful Voyager 1 team. Hopefully the mission will surpass its half-a-century birthday in space, coming right up next year.

#6455. Earthquake Faults Can Suddenly Become Almost As Fluid as Water, Study Finds

Scientists have uncovered evidence of an unexpected process that may allow earthquake faults to slip enormous distances.

Rocks along Japan’s Boso Peninsula have preserved evidence of an extraordinary process that may occur during powerful earthquakes. Researchers discovered ancient fault structures suggesting that clay trapped between moving rock surfaces became nearly as fluid as water, potentially allowing the fault to slip enormous distances with little resistance.

The findings, from a research team led by Professor Tetsuro Hirono of Osaka Metropolitan University, could help explain how some earthquakes produce the massive seafloor movements capable of triggering devastating tsunamis.

The researchers examined exposed rocks that formed in an ancient seafloor environment approximately 15 million years ago. Within an old earthquake fault, they identified unusual wavy and curved layers, along with swirling structures resembling vortices formed by moving fluids.

The team described these formations as “turbulent-flow-like.” Using fluid dynamics to analyze their shapes, the scientists found evidence that a process called thermal pressurization had caused clay within the fault to become fluidized.

Thermal pressurization occurs when rapid movement along a fault generates intense frictional heat. As water trapped in microscopic spaces within the rock heats up, pressure increases, reducing the frictional resistance that normally keeps the fault surfaces locked together. This weakening can allow much greater movement during an earthquake.

“Our analysis suggests that the viscosity approached that of water,” Professor Hirono explained. “This would have been a dramatic reduction. The fluidized state would have acted as a form of dynamic lubrication, causing the fault to weaken dramatically. The resulting large-scale slip would have produced a large displacement on the fault near the seafloor, potentially causing a tsunami.”

The mechanism could help explain the extreme seafloor displacement associated with some major earthquakes. In 2011, a magnitude 9.1 earthquake struck eastern Japan, with shaking and fault rupture lasting nearly six minutes. The earthquake shifted the ocean floor enough to generate a devastating tsunami. Although the ancient rocks do not establish whether the same weakening process occurred in 2011, they provide physical evidence of how faults may undergo dramatic changes during seismic events.

The researchers hope to apply their analytical methods to modern faults, using changes in the viscosity of fault materials to better estimate how far those faults might slip during an earthquake. More accurate assessments of fault movement could improve estimates of potential seafloor displacement and associated tsunami hazards.

“Understanding the change in viscosity in fault-slips may allow us to more accurately recognize the magnitude of fault slips, which would support tsunami mitigation efforts,” Professor Hirono concluded.

Reference: “Coseismic turbulence-like flow of fault material along the shallow portion of a plate-subduction-related fault” by Tatsuru Fukuta and Tetsuro Hirono, 27 June 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-57630-y

#6454. Where to Find the Fastest Delivery for the iPhone Duo

Apple picking is an annual autumn rite, but when it comes to shopping Apple’s first folding phone, retailers have mostly bare branches.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Apple sure underestimated how many people would scramble for an iPhone Duo. Tsunamis of anticipation over the first folding iPhone had built up over years, long before Apple made it official and announced it on October 16, 2026, but how many people would rush to buy a smartphone that starts at $1,999?

It took hardly a day to find out. Perhaps it had something to do with us declaring it the best folding phone yet. During the week prior to the iPhone Duo’s October 23 launch day, when those with a taste for Apple’s latest phone could preorder it on Apple.com, the ship date list stretched into January as people gobbled up the early batch of available units. And on launch day itself, local news everywhere ran story after story about long lines outside Apple stores, with many going home empty-handed before closing time as the Duo quickly sold out.

You can walk into an Apple store and try your luck, although I wouldn’t count on walking out with one in hand. Many Apple stores I’ve checked in big cities have none available for pickup. You can still order one online at Apple, as long as you’re fine with waiting until January 25 to get yours.

You can find the iPhone Duo at Best Buy for Verizon and AT&T. Switching up the color between Night Sky (black) and Star White, or the storage capacity (256GB, 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB), or the carrier, does not change the December 22 shipping or pickup date.

Heading to your local cellular carrier’s retail store may be your best bet for landing an iPhone Duo before Christmas, but like with the Apple Store, I wouldn’t count on it. Verizon casts a wide net for its estimated ship date: December 12–30. Those ordered from T-Mobile won’t make the Christmas cut. As of today, the backordered phone shows a ship date of December 31-January 6. And AT&T may have the longest ship time of all, as its ordering pages offer shipping “As soon as January 6,” which hints that the 6th is the earliest you may expect your AT&T-linked iPhone Duo, but that it may come later.

Interestingly, no matter how I configured each one in any color and storage combination, the estimated ship dates at all three carriers stayed the same. In past years at Apple launches, devices with higher capacities (and correspondingly higher price tags) tended to be available sooner. Not so this time with the iPhone Duo. Just remember that if you buy a phone from one network, it’s not guaranteed to work on another. If you want an unlocked iPhone Duo that’ll work on any cellular network, you’ll have to order it from Apple and practice patience until it ships in early 2027.

Walmart has listed product pages for the iPhone Duo since Apple announced it, but I’ve yet to see anybody actually able to order one there. I’ve kept a near-daily eye on the Walmart page, though, and every combination of color, carrier, and storage option has been out of stock and unavailable to backorder since the iPhone Duo’s debut.

If you’re on the fence, don’t expect the waitlist to shorten while you wring your hands. Occasionally, ship dates for hot, newly released devices move up as retailers receive new batches, but I’ve been keeping a close eye on the iPhone Duo for the past three weeks and haven’t seen that happen at any retailer, including Apple itself. The ship dates we’ve provided here are current as of today. They can only get longer from here.

#6453. A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud emerges every day during spring and summer on Mars, a long wispy ribbon downwind of the Arsia Mons volcano. This image of the cloud was captured by a camera aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express mission.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

ESA, EHU (top); J. Hernández-Bernal et al/Nature Geoscience, 2026 (bottom)

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.

While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

#6452. Earth's Gravity May Have Kept the Early Moon's Volcanic Heart Beating

We typically think of the Moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an exception. That understanding is grounded in physics - the Moon should have cooled rapidly after forming when a huge protoplanet hit the early Earth around 4.5 billion years ago. But, some lunar material returned from the Changâe-5 mission was notably formed only around two billion years ago, yet appeared to be volcanic in origin. So how did a world that was supposed to have settled down without volcanism remain hot enough to create these materials more than two billion years after its violent birth? A new paper from Miao Chen of the Chengdu University of Technology and his colleagues, and recently published in the journal Planet, offers an explanation - tidal heating.

Letâs first set the stage of the Moonâs creation. Our best guess is that it was created when another early protoplanet, named Theia, slammed into Earth in a massive collision, creating a chunk of debris that coalesced into the Moon. However, that amount of debris was relatively small - only about a quarter the size of the Earth itself, which meant the internal heat generated during its formation would rapidly radiate away, turning the Moon itself geologically dormant.

But when Changâe-5 returned some lunar basalts from Oceanus Procellarum back to Earth, laboratory dating showed them to be only around two billion years old. Basalts are only formed in active volcanoes, or other environments with similarly high pressures and temperatures. Environments that, at least according to traditional geological theory, shouldnât have existed on the Moon two billion years ago.

Fraser explains why the Moon is moving farther away.

Despite that, scientists have tried offering other solutions. Radioactive elements, such as potassium and uranium, emit some heat as they decay. But there wasnât enough un-decayed material left on the Moon to offer the amount of heat needed to form basalt two billion years ago. Asteroid strikes could cause localized high impact thermal spikes, but the heavy bombardment period that gave the Moon most of its craters had ended long before the basalt was formed.

So instead the authors turned to gravity - specifically to a phenomenon called tidal heating. This happens when a celestial body is squeezed, stretched, and kneaded as it travels in an elliptical orbit around a larger parent body. Perhaps the most famous example of this in the solar system is Io. This moon of Jupiter is constantly erupting due to the tidal squishing it undergoes during its orbit around the largest planet.

Obviously, the Moon doesnât seem to be undergoing any such squishing currently. However, two billion years ago, the Moon was much closer to the Earth than it is today, orbiting our planet in sixteen days rather than the twenty seven it takes now. Its orbit was also much more eccentric, looking much more like an oval than a circle. All of which means that Earth itself exerted huge rhythmic tidal forces on the Moon' s interior during the course of its orbit.

Fraser details Tidal Locking, which also affects the Moons geology.

Weâve known that for awhile, but astronomers have always modeled the Moon as a mostly uniform sphere when trying to understand how these gravitational squeezes affected it. However, scientists knew this was a simplification - there is an ultra-low viscosity zone of rock wrapping itself between the Moonâs core and mantle. When the research team plugged a more realistic 3D representation of the mantle setup into a convection simulation, they noticed that a ton of energy was directed specifically at two symmetric regions along the lunar core-mantle boundary.

These regions, which they named Tidal Heating Anomaly Zones (THAZs) , absorbed a huge amount of energy. They calculated that, around 3.2 billion years ago, despite taking up only 2.5% of the mantleâs total volume, the tidal strain on these regions delivered 150 gigawatts of power - more than four times the amount of energy generated by radioactive decay.

This seemed to be the driving force behind much of the Moonâs geological history. It helped keep the lunar core warm, which helped sustain a magnetic field for much longer the models originally predicted (and was a puzzle when scientists realized that Apollo lunar samples seemed to have formed in a strong magnetic field). It also drove huge mantle plumes that swelled toward the crust. Billions of years later, long after the tidal engine has calmed down, those stranded pockets of mantle melted to produce the basalts seen in the Changâe-5 samples.

If thereâs one thing thatâs clear from the paperâs theory, it's that we still donât know a lot about the Moonâs geological history. This new model offers some elegant answers to some of the most persistent questions in that area, but as of now itâs still only a theory. Maybe some of the numerous lunar missions planned over the next decade will be able to provide more definitive data to finally solve the evolutionary questions of our nearest neighbor.

#6451. The Secret to Saving Shellfish From Acidifying Oceans Could Be Hiding in Crushed Shells

Crushed shells helped young clams grow larger shells in laboratory tests, showing how a long-standing Indigenous coastal practice can offer local protection against ocean acidification.

For a young clam, the surrounding water can threaten the shell it is trying to grow. When seawater absorbs excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes more acidic, making shell growth more difficult and energetically costly for animals such as clams, oysters, and mussels. Acidic seawater can even dissolve shells. Larvae and juveniles are thought to be especially vulnerable to this process, known as ocean acidification.

Indigenous communities have long added crushed shells to coastal sands to help keep these ecosystems healthy. Research from the University of California, Davis now helps explain how this material, called shell hash, can protect young clams from some of acidification’s effects. Published in Biogeosciences, the study connects the chemistry of water between sand grains with changes in clam growth and gene activity.

At the UC Davis Bodega Marine Laboratory, researchers raised baby Pacific littleneck clams in four conditions. Two groups burrowed in sediment beneath either non-acidified or acidified seawater. The other two experienced the same seawater conditions, but their sediment contained shell hash. During the 90-day experiment, the team tracked shell growth and sampled the seawater three times a week, monitoring acidity, salinity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen.

“We found that, on average, clams grew larger shells when shell hash was present in their treatment,” said study first author Hannah Kempf, an environmental scientist at the California State Water Board who graduated from UC Davis with a Ph.D. in earth and planetary sciences in 2024. “Interestingly, we also found that, on a genetic level, the ‘acidification’ signal was dramatically minimized when shell hash was present.”

The crushed shells altered the chemistry of the water filling the tiny spaces between sand particles, reducing its overall acidity and creating better conditions for shell growth. That finding places the protection at a very local scale, in the water surrounding the burrowing clams.

“Adding crushed shells removed the negative genetic changes that occur when young clams are raised in acidified water,” said study corresponding author David Gold, an associate professor of earth and planetary sciences at UC Davis.

To examine gene activity, the researchers collected samples of the clams’ mantle tissue, which produces their shells, after 90 days and used them for follow-up gene sequencing. The analysis revealed gene expression profiles, or patterns of activity across genes. In clams raised in acidified seawater with shell hash, those profiles were largely indistinguishable from those of clams raised in non-acidified water.

“This was the first time the question was studied from a genetic perspective,” Gold said.

Traditional ecological knowledge provides significant evidence that shell hash benefits shell-making animals, said study co-author Tsim Schneider, an associate professor of anthropology at UC Santa Cruz. In the Pacific Northwest, some Indigenous communities build large-scale structures that expand intertidal spaces, the areas of shore between high and low tide. These structures promote habitat for invertebrates and other marine organisms.

“For me, one of the interesting aspects of this research is the potential to engage more fully with tribes on designing projects that promote their long-standing expertise and Indigenous science,” said Schneider, who is also affiliated with the National Science Foundation’s Center for Braiding Indigenous Knowledges and Science. “If there’s a history of adding shell hash to clam beds in California, for example, western science might be able to better support communities interested in reawakening dormant cultural knowledge and coastal stewardship practices.”

Reference: “Shell hash promotes growth in Pacific littleneck clams (Leukoma staminea) by altering pore water chemistry” by Hannah L. Kempf, Alyssa J. Griffin, Gabriel Ng, Tessa M. Hill, Tsim D. Schneider, Sandra J. Carlson and David A. Gold, 29 October 2026, Biogeosciences. DOI: 10.5194/bg-23-7627-2026

The research was supported by a California Sea Grant and the Russell J. and Dorothy S. Bilinski Fellowship.

#6450. Can We Build Life From Scratch? A First-of-Its-Kind Cell Is Raising New Questions About the Edge of Existence

The 36-gene cell can copy its DNA and divide—but its creator still doesn’t consider it alive.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

It was a sunny day on Stanford’s campus when, by Drew Endy’s reckoning, everything changed. During a May 2025 synthetic biology meeting that Endy, a synthetic biologist at Stanford, had co-organized, his friend and fellow researcher Kate Adamala pulled him aside to show him some of her lab’s recent results.

Adamala, a synthetic biologist at the University of Minnesota, brought up six sequential images of a synthetic cell on her laptop screen; her lab had constructed it and coaxed it into carrying out some of the key functions of natural cells. With some assistance, the lab-made cells were able to make proteins based on instructions in their minimal genome, to copy the DNA in that genome, to package bits of that copied DNA in new cells.

Endy believed Adamala’s results had revolutionized their field. During a recent Zoom call, he showed me why, sharing a video of one of his own lab’s projects, a perfectly round blob he says took six years to build. “This object is capable of expressing any DNA we add to it, and so since 2021 the puzzle was, what DNA do we add to this object to get it to grow and divide?” he says. “For about a decade I have been looking at objects like this that do not grow and divide,” so seeing Adamala’s cell, soon to be dubbed SpudCell, was “a holy moly moment,” he continues. Then, he flips to a slide with a picture of the Wright brothers’ airplane. It, too, was very limited, he notes. “It’s just barely a plane, and this is like, SpudCell’s just barely a cell. But it is.”

Synthetic biology is where biology meets engineering, often in an attempt to design biological systems to perform functions natural life does not, such as churning out medications, fuels, and other useful chemicals. Adamala and Endy hope that in the coming decades, it will pave the way to a resilient world of abundance in which essential resources can be produced locally, anywhere. For them, SpudCell is the seed from which that vision can grow. Along the way, the synthetic cell is providing a new lens on what exactly life is.

Adamala, Endy, and many other synthetic biologists believe their field will advance much faster if they work on a common system—picture many teams writing software for the same computer operating system, versus each having to build its own hardware and software from scratch. But prior to SpudCell, there’d been no such operating system for synthetic biologists to use. So the two began laying the groundwork to bring other synthetic biologists together to work on their own projects with SpudCell as a shared chassis, a project dubbed Biotic. Investor Chris Raggio agreed to provide $10 million as a philanthropic donation to the effort. Meanwhile, Adamala and her team continued working to improve SpudCell, and to publish a paper describing it.

After a top journal rejected the manuscript—ironically enough, it was Cell—Adamala realized that Biotic’s timeline didn’t have room for the months required to go through the submission, peer review, and revision process again. So, she posted it online herself on the preprint server bioXriv, which doesn’t require peer review, and sent out a press release. “That was actually the hardest decision for me because I’ve never done a big deal about a preprint before I knew it’s going to get published,” she says. (The group has since re-submitted the paper for publication in a different journal.)

The paper went live on the lab’s website the next day, on July 1, 2026. As the stories on SpudCell rolled in from the news—among them The New York Times (twice), CNN, STAT, and Science—Adamala was apprehensive. “Seriously every morning, I was waking up terrified that I’m going to see an email that points out the fatal flaw in the paper. That’s supposed to be the point of peer review, and now it was like publicly peer-reviewed. Everyone got to see it.” That email never came.

Adamala grew up in a small town in Poland. She learned to pilot small planes before she learned to drive. Flying is a hobby, “but it’s also kind of a mindset to me,” Adamala says. “You think about safety, you think about ways to do things, and you also think about engineering even if you’re not an engineer.”

In graduate school, Adamala worked on research questions related to how rudimentary life might have evolved on Earth—or elsewhere. But while the work gave her a conversation-starting answer to the “what do you do?” question at parties, she “thought it would be nice to do something useful for a change,” she says. Something that her grandma could use. So she completed a postdoc in synthetic neurobiology. “I learned that I don’t like neurobiology, but I did learn that I like doing useful things,” she continues.

Adamala moved into synthetic biology, at first with the idea of using the field’s tools to modify naturally evolved life. But she soon adjusted course as she realized that biology is “such a black box. We don’t understand the whole cell,” she explains. To truly understand a cell and successfully engineer it, she decided, it would instead need to be built from the bottom up.

Work on what would become the SpudCell began shortly before the COVID-19 pandemic. The project drew on components already developed in Adamala’s lab or by others, and included a cell membrane made of fat molecules surrounding a watery inside with a tiny, 36-gene genome and the specialized proteins needed to make new proteins based on the genes’ instructions. Putting it all together was a slow process of “trial and error—mostly error,” Adamala says. Her team developed a system for feeding the artificial cells the molecules they’d need to grow and carry out reactions, including fats and building blocks of DNA and proteins.

Once that was working, “I was actually ready to call it a day,” Adamala says. “But then I got this idea of getting the replication to work and . . . that delayed everything again forever.” The ability to replicate itself—that is, to reproduce—would be a critical step toward making the SpudCell more lifelike. The team ended up adding specialized proteins to the cells’ environment that stuck to the cell membranes. When enough proteins stud the membrane, they repel each other, forcing part of the surface to bud off and form a new cell.

By early 2024, images indicated that Adamala’s team was able to coax the cells through five cycles of growth and replication. But such visual data can be deceptive, so the team ran tests that allowed them to compare the amount of DNA the cells had started with to the amount after five generations. They showed the SpudCells really had been making copies of their own genomes. This was the moment, Adamala remembers, when she thought, “oh wow, this actually works.”

The replication was far from perfect. The cell’s genome is split up into seven round segments called plasmids, each copied separately, and whether each of the daughter cells ended up with a complete set of these plasmids is a matter of chance. Another awkward feature of the cells is that they couldn’t make their own ribosomes, the crucial factories that churn out new proteins; those needed to be supplied via the feeding system.

The system requires “very intensive cellular CPR,” notes Robert Dorit, an evolutionary biologist at Smith College who was not involved in the work. “They have to supply a lot of stuff from the outside. They have to create a set of very particular conditions, and those conditions need to be constantly reinforced.” Nevertheless, he says features such as the ability to divide and pass down genetic material make SpudCell a considerable advancement. Adamala’s group has, he says, “raised the bar for what they’re willing to call a minimal cell, and I think that’s really great.”

At Biotic’s first meeting, its founders were looking to bring their colleagues together around SpudCell as a common system, to work on modules that can be added onto it while maintaining interoperability. Their vision is to achieve truly world-changing innovations via synthetic biology by 2050. One of these, according to Adamala, is replacing petrochemicals—everything from jet fuel to synthetic fabrics—with chemicals produced by engineered organisms, potentially remaking the world economy and slicing the cost of energy, fertilizer, and other products downstream from oil. Other possibilities are decentralizing production of food and medication. At the kickoff meeting, Adamala showed a slide with a hypothetical cell that would live inside a patient, producing a therapy when it receives a signal indicating illness.

Not all synthetic biologists are in it for the applications—at least, not primarily. Some are pursuing questions about the very origins of life, much as Adamala did during her PhD work. Humans have long sought to understand what life is and what differentiates it from nonliving matter, says Roseanna Zia, an engineering professor at the University of Missouri. One approach to answering that question is to build life, she adds. “I want to build a computational model so that we can replicate whatever it is that makes things transition from the nonliving chemistry and physics to this thing that we call life.” Her group is also working on a model of SpudCell that could ultimately help other researchers to fine-tune the synthetic cell and design it to carry out the kind of functions Adamala envisions.

It’s worth noting that not only has science yet to come up with a comprehensive mechanism for how life might have first arisen on Earth; there’s also disagreement over where exactly the line between life and non-life lies. In the wake of SpudCell’s unveiling, Adamala says she heard from many people who consider it to be alive. She disagrees. “Definitions of life are arbitrary,” Adamala says. Her own definition is more of a gut feeling than a scientific set of benchmarks, but by her reckoning, SpudCell is not (yet) alive because it’s not robust enough; it can only replicate a handful of times before it grinds to a halt.

In addition to exactly what life is and how it came about, there’s the question of how it might have looked had it evolved differently at the start. Juan Pérez-Mercader, an astrobiologist at Harvard University, leads work to create systems that mimic functions of living organisms, entirely from nonbiological chemicals. The hope is that “the study of these very simple systems can lead you to understand better what to expect … in terms of potential life outside the Earth,” as well as from artificial life, he says.

Of course, when many people think of human-made life, extraterrestrial microbes aren’t top of mind, much less visions of a petrochemical-free future of abundance. Start with Frankenstein’s monster and carry through to Jeff Goldblum intoning “Life finds a way” shortly before velociraptors and a T-rex break containment. For those keeping track of less cinematic “what if?” scenarios, there’s mirror life, the so-far-only-hypothesized prospect that cells could be built of biomolecules that are a flipped, mirror image of those in existing, natural life forms. Such organisms would evade detection by our non-mirror immune systems, the thinking goes, and easily kill us and wreak ecological havoc.

What is needed to ensure the safety of synthetic biology work and head off bad actors who would use its technologies for ill? Several sessions at Biotic’s kickoff addressed this question. In one, Adamala said her group is “designing this technology with firewalls, with kill switches, with technologies that allow us to keep it safe from the beginning. So we’re not retrofitting safety.” Endy later acknowledged that “No answer relative to biosecurity today should be satisfying. We have not secured biology's domain.” Biotic won’t be able to do so alone, he added.

Both Adamala and Endy prefer to focus their “what ifs” on the positive developments they see arising from the technology. Endy cites a survey of first-year Stanford undergraduates about how they expect humanity to be faring when they’re middle-aged, relative to today. “The majority of our students say the 2050s are going to be worse, and they have very limited confidence that any of the grown-ups are going to do anything that matters,” he says. “That’s unacceptable to me, and shame on us if we don’t act to bend the future toward something more positive.”

Biotic has set a countdown to a target date of January 1, 2050, dubbed Bloomsday, to bring about a bioeconomy, in part to inspire people to take part in building that future. The name is a counter to the Doomsday Clock.

“For the first time in modern history, we can practically imagine making things work really well,” Endy says. “And that’s going to be extraordinarily challenging to pull off, but not impossible.”

Shawna Williams is a freelance writer and editor based in Queens, NY. Her work has appeared in publications including The Scientist, BioSpace, and Nautilus.

#6449. Could Type 2 Diabetes Be Reversed? 14-Year Study Reveals Remarkable Results

In a long-term trial, weight-loss surgery led to more type 2 diabetes remissions than intensive medical and lifestyle management, while patients’ disease histories offered clues to who might benefit most.

For some people with type 2 diabetes, keeping blood sugar under control without medication is possible. This state, known as remission, raises a question that could shape years of treatment decisions: Which approaches give people the best chance of reaching it, and what makes it more likely to last?

A long-term study found that 58% of participants assigned to weight-loss surgery achieved remission during follow-up, compared with 3% of those assigned to intensive medical and lifestyle management. Participants were followed for a median of 11 years, with some followed for up to 14 years. Those percentages describe how many people reached remission, rather than how many remained in remission throughout that time.

Researchers analyzed data from 262 people with type 2 diabetes, including 166 assigned to metabolic-bariatric surgery, commonly called weight-loss surgery, and 96 assigned to medical and lifestyle management. They defined remission as an A1C below 6.5% without blood sugar-lowering medication. A1C is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The findings were published in Diabetes Care, a journal of the American Diabetes Association®. They come from the Alliance of Randomized Trials of Medicine vs. Metabolic Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes (ARMMS-T2D), the largest, longest-running trial of metabolic surgery for diabetes. The study’s lead author is Donald Simonson, M.D., MPH, Sc.D., of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston.

Participants who had lived with diabetes for fewer years, did not use insulin, and took fewer types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment were more likely to achieve remission. Greater weight loss during the first year after treatment was also associated with a higher likelihood of remission.

Among people who initially reached remission, diabetes was more likely to return in those who had lived with the disease longer and those who took more types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment. Together, these associations suggest that a patient’s diabetes history and response to treatment may help physicians assess both the likelihood of remission and its potential duration.

The study’s principal investigator, John P. Kirwan, Ph.D., was named executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center this summer. He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the University of Oklahoma and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

“For years, one of the most consequential questions in diabetes care has been whether the benefits of metabolic surgery endure,” Kirwan said. “Now we have a durable answer. Over 14 years, 58% of surgical patients achieved remission, compared with just 3% on medication and lifestyle alone. By identifying who is most likely to achieve lasting remission, including shorter diabetes duration, no insulin use, and greater early weight loss, we can offer surgery to the right people earlier, rather than as a last resort.”

Kirwan has led the study since its inception, through his years at the Cleveland Clinic and the Pennington Biomedical Research Center at Louisiana State University. He now brings his expertise in translational and clinical research to the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus.

“Recruiting Dr. Kirwan to lead the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center brings to Oklahoma one of the world’s foremost authorities on long-term treatment for type 2 diabetes,” said Gary Raskob, Ph.D., Senior Vice President and Provost of the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “Research of this caliber is exactly what this center, and Harold Hamm’s investment in it, was created to advance.”

Reference: “Predictors of Type 2 Diabetes Remission and Relapse After Metabolic-Bariatric Surgery or Medical-Lifestyle Therapy in the ARMMS-T2D Study” by Donald C. Simonson, David E. Cummings, Philip R. Schauer, Ali Aminian, Bo Hu, David E. Arterburn, John M. Jakicic, Sangeeta R. Kashyap, Ashley H. Vernon, William F. Gourash, Anita P. Courcoulas, Mary Elizabeth Patti and John P. Kirwan, 20 October 2026, Diabetes Care. DOI: 10.2337/dc26-1070

A Roman-era belt buckle discovered in a Ukrainian forest hints at the ancient conflict between the Romans and the Dacians.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Ukraine have found a colorful belt buckle that may have been worn by a nomadic equestrian warrior 1,800 years ago on the fringes of the Roman Empire.

The belt buckle was unearthed by local residents in the Tsetsyn Forest in southeastern Ukraine and given to Antonii Moisei, a professor at Bukovinian State Medical University, according to a translated statement. The roughly square metal buckle, which is about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) on each side, has teal, blue and yellow enamel decorations.

The style of the decoration and the metal construction place the creation of the buckle in the second to third centuries A.D., when this part of Ukraine was in the ancient province of Roman Dacia, according to Moisei.

The column that the Roman emperor Trajan erected in Rome following the empire's triumph in the Dacian Wars.

Under Emperor Trajan, Rome fought the Dacian Wars (A.D. 101-102 and 105-106) against the denizens of the Dacian kingdom and its leader, Decebalus. Roman legions destroyed Dacia and annexed it as a new province. Trajan celebrated his victory in Rome, complete with a famous column that depicts details of the Dacian Wars.

In addition to the buckle, Moisei collected a decorative belt fitting and three small, round metal objects that probably belonged to the same belt. Moisei created a reconstruction of what the belt might have looked like before it was lost in the forest nearly two millennia ago.

But it's unclear who lost the belt. One of Moisei's theories is that the belt belonged to a horse-riding Sarmatian warrior originally from the Black Sea region. The Sarmatians were a group of tribes that lived outside the borders of the Roman Empire, in what are now central Ukraine, southern Russia and the Balkans. While some Sarmatian warriors fought against the incursion of the Roman Empire, others fought with Rome as mercenaries.

The metal belt fragments are part of a Roman provincial craft tradition, according to the statement, and they may have been obtained through trade or as a trophy of war. But Moisei is still studying the artifacts to confirm whether they were Sarmatian. Either way, the military belt provides new evidence of Roman military contact on the outskirts of the empire, and future work could help experts understand how the Romans interacted with the local Dacians during wartime.

#6447. NASA's Twin Spacecraft Will Execute Powered Slingshot Maneuvers on Their Way to Mars

A pair of NASA are spacecraft are about to perform a slingshot maneuver above Earth, and some of us might get to see them. They're on their way to Mars, where they'll dig more deeply into one of the Solar System's puzzles: how Mars lost its ancient atmosphere. The pair are unique, because once they reach the planet, they'll be the first spacecraft to "fly" in formation around Mars.

It's becoming clear, if not certain, that Mars was once warm and wet. It may have been habitable, even inhabited by simple life. But something happened and the planet is now cold and dead.

To be warm and wet, it must have had a much thicker atmosphere than the thin, CO2 atmosphere it has now. Scientists who study the iron-red world postulate that UV radiation from the Sun drove Mars' ancient atmosphere into space. That only happened after Mars' molten core cooled, and the planet lost its protective magnetic field. Once exposed to the full force of the Sun's UV radiation, the atmosphere was doomed.

Though its global magnetosphere is long gone, Mars still has patches of magnetic fields called crustal magnetic fields, or remnant magnetic fields. They aren't created by a dynamo; they're local magnetic fields generated by iron-rich chunks of the planet's crust. When Mars' dynamo failed billions of years ago, these chunks locked-in the magnetic orientation of the ancient crust. These surface fields on Mars also generate similar patches of magnetic fields in the planet's upper atmosphere. All these fields aren't anywere near as strong as the ancient dynamo, but they're enough to work with.

This map of Mars' crustal magnetism was created with data from NASA's now-defunct Mars Global Surveyor. In simple terms, it's a colour-coded map of the magnetic strength. Blue is weak, red is strong. Image Credit: By NASA - Public Domain.

While the broad picture of Mars' atmosphere loss is clear, the gritty details are not. The NASA spacecraft on their way to orbit Mars are called Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE). They're twins, named Red and Blue, and they'll measure how the solar wind interacts with the remnants of Mars' ancient magnetic field.

Soon the spacecraft will approach Earth. At their closest, they'll be between about 965 to 1,770 kilometers above the surface, and they'll use their thrusters to boost their speed. Those boosts will combined with Earth's gravity, and they'll slingshot their way to Mars. The first will do so on November 7th, the second on November 9th. These trans-Mars injection burns will last about 9 minutes and will increase their speed from about 10.14 km/s to 10.78 km/s. That's an increase of more than 2,000 km/hour.

These maneuvers are necessary because ESCAPADE didn't launch in the usual Mars launch window. Those windows occur about every 26 months. So the spacecraft had to loiter near the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2 for a while, then approach Earth and use these burns to power their way to Mars. This led to some bonus science, where the spacecraft flew through and observed Earth's magnetotail. They were the first spacecraft to do so, and those observations will be shared soon.

A natural question arises about ESCAPADE: Why are there two spacecraft?

Solar wind interactions with magnetic fields can change on very short timescales. A single spacecraft wouldn't be able to tell if changes it observes are due to changes in these interactions, or changes in its position. A pair of spacecraft flying in formation removes this uncertainty. NASA calls this formation the "String of Pearls."

This animation shows the ESCAPADE spacecraft in their String of Pearls formation above Mars.

The spacecraft will fly the same orbit at varying distances from each other. But that's just for the first part of the mission, Science Phase A, which will last about 6 months. In Science Phase B, ESCAPADE's Blue and Red units will work more independently. Blue will lower its orbit to about 7,000 km and Red will raise its orbit to about 10,000 km. That will last about 5 months, until the end of ESCAPADE's nominal science mission. The spacecraft should remain in operation for many years after that, and NASA will have some decisions to make then.

The spacecraft will be visible to some observers on the ground, though a telescope will almost certainly be needed. They'll present as a pair of dim, refrigerator-sized objects moving against the starry background. Not super-exciting, but interesting nonetheless.

It's eerie to think about a planet like Mars losing its habitability and dying. It tells us something about the search for life, and about Earth. There may be multitudes of planets that were habitable for short periods of timeâmaybe hosting simple lifeâthat were extinguished before any complexity could arise. It puts life on Earth in perspective for its rarity. Earth has been habitable for billions of years, and, against probabilities, complex life has fluorished for hundreds of millions of years, even longer depending on which definition is used.

Having one of these extinguished planets next door is a rare opportunity to understand how this happens, and ESCAPADE will take full advantage of that opportunity.

#6445. Kids Who Learn To Swim Early May Have an Unexpected Advantage in School

Children who learn to swim early may have a head start in classroom skills, with research finding developmental advantages even after accounting for socioeconomic background.

When family budgets tighten, swimming lessons can be among the first expenses to go. Most swim schools operate as commercial businesses, and cost is the biggest barrier to participation. Yet the consequences of missing out may extend beyond water safety and fitness to the skills children need when they start school.

A four-year study involving nearly 7,000 survey respondents and individual testing of 177 children suggests that children who learn to swim early have developmental advantages over their peers. Participants younger than 5 could be 5 to 18 months ahead of typical milestones in literacy, numeracy, and following instructions compared with the general population of children their age. Those advantages remained when socioeconomic background was taken into account.

Robyn Jorgensen, Emeritus Professor at the University of Canberra in Australia, examines and expands on the research in her new book, Why Young Children Should Learn to Swim.

Jorgensen does not interpret the findings as evidence that children who learn to swim are innately smarter. Instead, she argues that lessons develop skills and habits children can carry into the classroom. A child counting kicks from one to ten with an instructor, for example, is practicing number sequencing and one-to-one correspondence, matching each number to a single action.

The project grew out of a conversation between Jorgensen and Laurie Lawrence, an Olympic swim coach inducted into both the Australian and U.S. Swimming Halls of Fame. Lawrence thought children who learned to swim early generally seemed more “school-ready.”

“There was no formal evidence to support this observation, but it was one that Laurie felt he and many others in the swim industry observed,” Jorgensen explains.

To investigate that “industry hunch,” Jorgensen and her colleagues used the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales and Woodcock-Johnson III assessments. These internationally recognized testing tools were normed against national census data, providing reference standards for comparing the children’s performance with that of the wider population.

The results surprised even Jorgensen, who said, “My early observations of the young learners piqued my interest while retaining some sense of skepticism about what could be achieved. I am not from a swimming background, so had no vested interest in the ‘proving’ or otherwise of Laurie’s hunch. My only interest in swimming was as a grandparent and around water safety for my children and grandchildren, and as a recreational activity.”

Beyond the literacy and numeracy findings, the research suggests that early swimming participants are more sociable and have measurable advantages in cognitive development, language skills, and emotional regulation. These findings point to potential benefits for academic success.

“It is reasonable to claim that swimming prepares children for the schooling years, particularly the early years and the transition into schooling,” Jorgensen explains.

Access to those potential benefits is sharply unequal. Jorgensen’s analysis identifies the United States and China as having the greatest inequities in access, with regular swimming lessons affordable only to very affluent families. Singapore, Australia, Brazil, and South Africa also face substantial economic and geographic barriers.

One respondent from Zimbabwe described how lessons compete with basic necessities. “So swimming is still seen in Africa in general as elite. But basically, if you are a working-level person well below average, swimming lessons will not be a priority; what will be a priority is feeding your family.”

Even reaching a pool can be difficult. In Australia, families on remote farming properties can face journeys of hundreds of kilometers to the nearest one. The study describes “a double whammy” for children from low-income and rural communities, who are both the least likely to have access to lessons and the most at risk of drowning.

With cost-of-living pressures affecting families worldwide, Jorgensen is calling for broader government support. She argues that governments have both a moral and a financial incentive to intervene, given the billions they already spend trying to close gaps in school achievement.

“What this study has shown is that even when socioeconomic backgrounds are accounted for, children who participate in quality lessons achieve better than the general population. It would make sense for the government to consider investing in providing or subsidizing early years swimming for families who would otherwise be excluded from participation in early years swimming lessons,” Jorgensen explains.

“Investing in quality swimming lessons would make a politically wise move. The cost of lessons can be quite high, but if policies were created to offer subsidies for parents or to create swim programs for disadvantaged families, there is considerable potential for adding capital to these cohorts of learners,” she explains.

Reference: “Why Young Children Should Learn to Swim: Learnings from Participation in Early Years Swimming” by Robyn Jorgensen, 18 November 2026, Routledge. DOI: 10.4324/9781003774747

#6444. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

This story was updated on October 29, 2026 to include expert input from Emma Stone.
