#6397. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

J.M. Young et al. Permafrost detachment slides: a distinct high‐magnitude permafrost mass wasting process. Geophysical Research Letters. 2026. doi: 10.1029/2026GL124103

J.M. Young et al. Recent intensification (2004 – 2020) of permafrost mass‐wasting in the central Mackenzie Valley foothills is a legacy of past forest fire disturbances. Geophysical Research Letters. 2022. doi: 10.1029/2022GL100559

#6395. The 9 Best Ductless Air Conditioners for Efficient Home Cooling

Whether you want a budget-friendly option or a high-efficiency heat pump for year-round comfort, these are the best ductless air conditioners to consider right now.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Tired of using loud and unsightly window air conditioners or clunky and underpowered portable air conditioners? Even if you don’t have the means to install a fully ducted HVAC system in your home, you can still upgrade to a more powerful cooling system with a ductless air conditioner.

Ductless air conditioners, often called mini-splits, cool targeted areas of your home without relying on the ductwork. Instead, they connect a compact outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers, which are usually mounted on a wall or ceiling.

To help narrow down the best ductless air conditioners, I compared models across capacity, efficiency, installation requirements, noise level, smart features, and overall value. I also spoke with HVAC expert Kim Lincoln, who has 25 years of industry experience, for guidance on how mini-splits work, when they make sense, and what shoppers should know before buying.

To ensure that our list of ductless air conditioners caters to a wide range of needs, I looked at units from well-respected brands like Pioneer and Senville and selected models of various sizes at different prices. Many come with features like programmability, dehumidification settings, and, in a few instances, smartphone functionality.

As an added perk, most of these contraptions also double as heaters—which is useful during cooler months. I leaned on my experience with different types of cooling units, as well as product specs I reviewed during my research. The final list below represents the best in each category, including best budget and best for DIY installation.

For this update, I relied on the expertise of Lincoln, as well as my own experiences with several types of ductless air conditioners. I asked her a variety of questions about mini-splits, touching on topics like the differences between this type of air conditioner from other units, installation, and more. I also updated the products I recommend to reflect recent advances in smart home technology and energy efficiency.

This highly-rated AC unit from Senville comes in a number of sizes, ranging from 9,000 BTUs all the way up to 30,000 BTUs, and it comes in 120- and 230-volt models. It has 4-in-1 functionality, working as an air conditioner, heater, dehumidifier, and fan, and it operates at just 34 decibels, making it a tranquil option for a bedroom or nursery.

You can control all of its settings via the included remote. The air conditioner comes with an installation kit, including a communication cable and copper lines, but it’s important to note the brand requires professional installation for the unit’s five-year warranty to be valid.

This ductless air conditioner is perfect for small rooms and spaces, with a coverage that can handle areas between 200 and 500 square feet. Great for climate control storage and small bedrooms, the WYS009A-20 is an Energy Star-certified machine that’ll help you save money year-round. It cools as low as -13 degrees F and heats up to 122 F.

It has a permanent washable air filter and a remote control for easy operation—though you have to buy an additional remote to use Wi-Fi capabilities. It also operates at only 25 decibels, making it one of the quietest machines on this list, and it has four modes: cooling, heating, dehumidification, and ventilation. After installation, Pioneer provides free tech support and five-year coverage on replacement parts and the compressor.

This model from Della is a great value. It delivers 24,000 BTUs/hour, making it suitable for rooms up to 1,500 square feet. It’s also the sleekest model we found.

In addition to cooling, this unit has settings for heating, dehumidification, and ventilation, and that versatility extends to its selection of impressive features, including a 24-hour timer, sleep mode, energy-saving mode, and multiple fan speeds. You can easily adjust all of these using the included remote control and the Della+ app. The app allows users to control the settings, set timers, and control various Della units from one screen for whole-house control.

The Della Mini-Split comes with a full installation kit, including a line set, and it operates at 51 decibels. Some installers report the directions are confusing and have had to rely on online guides for extra help, but most reviewers are happy with this unit.

Suppose you want the ability to adjust your air conditioning from your smartphone. In that case, this model from Senville includes built-in Wi-Fi connectivity, allowing you to operate it remotely from an Android or iOS device.

It’s suitable for large spaces, thanks to its four-zone setup and 36,000-BTU output. Plus, it also has heating, dehumidification, and fan settings.

The unit has a turbo mode for even more versatility, and it automatically switches from cooling to heating based on the ambient temperature. The Senville Mini-Split comes with an installation kit that includes a 16-foot line set for your professional installer.

If you plan to install your ductless air conditioner in a large room, this model delivers 36,000 BTUs, making it powerful enough to efficiently cool spaces up to 1,500 square feet. It can be used for heating and cooling, operating in ambient temperatures between 5 and 122 degrees Fahrenheit, and it comes with a comprehensive installation kit.

You’ll get an insulated and pre-flared 25-foot line set, communication wires, a drainage extension, and remote control. The unit can even be equipped with wifi if you purchase the brand’s USB adapter (sold separately).

The large, rectangular indoor units that come with most ductless air conditioners can be a bit cumbersome on your wall, and if you prefer a more streamlined appearance, this unit uses a ceiling cassette instead.

The 9,000-BTU system can be used for heating and cooling in spaces up to 350 square feet, and it comes with a 16-foot line set and all necessary installation equipment. The system has a 24-hour timer, sleep mode, turbo function, and three indoor fan modes. It operates at 31.5 decibels, making it ideal for bedrooms.

If energy usage is your top priority, DELLA’s 12,000-BTU mini-split is one of the most efficient systems commonly available online. Its efficiency rating sits around 22–23 SEER2 (which is a newer efficiency standard that prioritizes real-world performance), and that means it uses significantly less electricity than many other entry-level mini-splits.

The inverter compressor automatically adjusts output instead of cycling on and off, which helps the unit maintain steady temperatures and reduces power consumption. (You’ll really notice this feature during periods of extreme weather that tend to spike utility bills.)

The unit is well-sized for bedrooms, offices, or small living areas, and it cools and heats spaces up to about 600 square feet. The built-in Wi-Fi control and quiet operation round out the package.

One drawback: While DELLA has great reviews, it’s a smaller company and may offer less customer support, based on some user feedback.

If you’re looking to cool a smaller space like a bedroom or home office, Costway Blast Series is a solid pick for a bedroom, office, or other small room where you want more permanent cooling than a window unit can provide. Its 9,000-BTU output is sized for spaces up to 450 square feet, so it’s a better fit for modest rooms than the larger 18,000- or 24,000-BTU systems in this category. It also offers quiet operation, a display-off function, a timer, and a remote control you can use from bed.

Like many of the units we looked at, this product is more versatile than a cooling-only AC, too. It has cooling, heating, dry, fan, and sleep modes, plus ECO, turbo, and iFEEL settings. The washable filter and self-cleaning function are also helpful for keeping routine maintenance manageable.

The tradeoff is that this model requires 208- to 230-volt power, so it may need electrical work before installation. Its 17 SEER2 efficiency rating is respectable, but not as high as some more expensive bedroom-friendly mini-splits. Still, for a smaller space, it offers a useful mix of performance, basic heat-pump functionality, and good value.

This high-efficiency mini-split system is specifically designed for DIY installation—and no special tools are required. It’s compatible with Google Assistant and Alexa, and it comes with features like an auto restart if there’s a power outage, leak detection, and sleep mode on the remote to adjust the temperature automatically during the night.

The unit heats and cools with 24,000 BTUs of power, which is more than enough, but considering the model's premium price, it's a little on the low side. Its SEER rating is 20.5, and operation is relatively quiet.

Overall, it’s a great package, albeit a pricey one.

Compared to window or portable air conditioners, ductless systems are more permanent, more powerful, and typically quieter. They also give you more control over specific rooms, so you can cool the spaces you actually use instead of the whole house at once. There are some drawbacks, though.

Ductless ACs run pricey (even setting aside the cost of installation). They’re also more visible than central air vents, and you need to size and place them carefully to cool a room evenly. DIY installs or wrong-sized units can cause issues in the long run.

Maintenance can also be difficult, as not all HVAC professionals are familiar with these products. However, for an older home with radiator heat (like mine is), it’s the best way to add efficient air conditioning without blocking most of our windows.

First, decide how many indoor units you need and where you’ll place them. Unlike window units, mini-split systems are permanent fixtures, so carefully consider where they’ll be most efficient within your home.

Generally, a single ductless air conditioner can handle cooling a targeted area or a single room. If you’re cooling down multiple rooms, consider a multi-zone system so that you get even temperatures throughout your home.

It’s also essential to select a unit that’s powerful enough for the room it’s in—too small and it may not cool your space. The cooling capacity of air conditioners is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTUs, per hour.

As a general rule of thumb, choose a unit that delivers 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. So, a 200-square-foot room needs at least a 4,000-BTU air conditioner. Those sensitive to noise should consider units with a quiet mode feature.

It’s also important to consider the electrical system in the area you plan to install the mini-split. Many larger mini-splits require 208- to 230-volt power, which works with both commercial 208V electrical service and the 240V circuits typically used for major appliances in homes, while smaller systems may run on standard 120V outlets without any needed upgrades.

Quieter units are more desirable for bedrooms, living rooms, and nurseries, where a peaceful environment is essential. Look for ductless air conditioners with noise levels between 19 and 30 decibels, since this range can be compared to the sound of leaves rustling or a soft whisper.

Units with levels between 30 to 40 decibels are still suitable for other areas of the home, since this range is comparable to background noise or casual conversation.

While shopping for your ductless air conditioner, you may see “SEER” with a number next to it. SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, which measures how much energy your air conditioner uses during the annual cooling season. The higher the SEER rating, the less energy your unit uses to cool your home.

You may also see “SEER2,” a newer efficiency standard introduced in 2023 that uses updated testing conditions meant to better reflect real-world performance. SEER2 numbers are typically slightly lower than SEER ratings for the same unit, but they represent the same idea: higher numbers mean more efficient energy usage.

A product with an Energy Star certification has been rigorously tested by the United States Environmental Protection Agency for its energy efficiency. EPA-recognized laboratories test products to Energy Star specifications to ensure manufacturers produce energy-saving products.

Although testing guidelines change per product category, all items must prove they consume less energy than standard models without compromising performance.

Mini-splits are more permanent and expensive than window or portable air conditioners, so they make the most sense when you plan to cool the same space for several seasons. Most systems also require professional installation, and larger units may need electrical upgrades before you can install them.

They’re also not invisible. The indoor air handler usually stays mounted high on the wall year-round, which may bother homeowners who prefer the low-profile look of central air vents. Proper sizing and placement matter, too, since an oversized, undersized, or poorly positioned unit can lead to uneven cooling, wasted energy, or poor humidity control.

Ductless air conditioners cool your home without using the network of ducts that central HVAC systems rely on, says Lincoln. “The way I explain ductless cooling to homeowners is simple: the system conditions the room directly instead of trying to send cooled air through ductwork first,” she explains.

Instead, ductless air conditioners connect a small outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers using refrigerant lines. Because there’s no ductwork involved, these types of units are often more efficient and easier to install in older homes, additions, or finished spaces where running ducts would be difficult. They also allow for “zoned” cooling, meaning you can control the temperature in individual rooms instead of conditioning the entire house at once.

These systems are also more customizable than a whole-house system. “Where mini-splits really shine is zoning,” explains Lincoln. “One outdoor unit can support multiple indoor heads, so different parts of the house can be conditioned based on how those spaces are actually used.”

Yes. “A mini-split is just a ductless system made up of an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor air handlers,” says Lincoln. The terms ductless air conditioner and mini-split are generally used interchangeably, as we have in this guide.

Both describe systems that pair an outdoor condenser with one or more indoor air handlers connected by refrigerant lines instead of ductwork. The “split” part refers to the system being divided between indoor and outdoor components.

Some mini-splits provide cooling only, but many modern models are actually heat pumps, meaning they can both cool and heat your home using the same system. Adding air conditioning to an older home that previously utilized radiator or baseboard heat can be tricky—squeezing ductwork into closets and unused corners feels a bit like remodelling Jenga. These units solve that issue without much fuss.

Usually, yes. In most cases, it makes sense to hire a professional. Installing a mini-split usually involves mounting indoor and outdoor units, running refrigerant lines, and making electrical connections, which is why many manufacturers recommend professional installation.

“Installation is where good equipment gets made—or wasted,” advises Lincoln. “Mini-splits look deceptively simple once they’re on the wall, but installation is not casual work. Line sets, electrical, drainage, vacuuming the system down properly before startup…those are the steps that determine whether the unit runs the way it was engineered to run.”

Some systems are more DIY-friendly, but even those can be complicated if you’re not comfortable working with electrical systems or HVAC equipment. Professional installation also helps ensure the system runs efficiently and may be required to maintain the manufacturer’s warranty. If you are a very seasoned DIY pro who’s handy with a YouTube tutorial, you might be okay. Otherwise, we recommend budgeting for an installer.

Companies size mini-splits systems based on BTUs, which measure how much heating or cooling power the unit can deliver.

“When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close. For a mini-split, a proper load calculation is the better answer.” This is another reason it’s great to work with an expert installer before ordering—they can guide your purchasing based on your needs.

Lincoln explains that it’s not a straightforward calculation, in most cases. “Room size is only the starting point. Sun exposure, ceiling height, insulation, window size, window direction, occupancy, and heat from electronics or appliances all change the cooling load,” she adds.

Smaller systems around 9,000 BTU often work for bedrooms or small offices, while 12,000–18,000-BTU systems handle larger living areas. As a rough rule, most homeowners look at units sized for the square footage of the space they want to heat or cool, but must consider all of these other factors, too.

Researchers used CT scans to crack a 400-year-old code and open a mysterious padlock that washed up in Wales with the Ann Francis treasure hoard.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Elizabethan padlock has been opened for the first time in more than 400 years after researchers used X-ray imaging techniques to crack its four-letter combination.

The brass lock was part of the Ann Francis treasure hoard, named after the British merchant ship that wrecked during a storm off the coast of Wales in 1583. Researchers believe the lock once secured a chest aboard the ship, before becoming separated from whatever riches it was protecting.

Some of the Ann Francis' cargo was recovered at the time of the wreck, while the rest was claimed by the sea. In recent decades, dredging and storms on Margam beach in South Wales have exposed some of the ship's lost treasure.

Between 1996 and 2017, metal detectorist Peter Hughes found the lock and much of the hoard, which included gold and silver coins. The lock was subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru — National Museum Wales, which worked with researchers at Cardiff University in Wales to decipher its combination.

To study the lock's internal mechanisms, the team used micro-CT scans, which make thousands of X-rays that can then be configured into a 3D digital image. By matching internal notches to external letters in the digital 3D image, the researchers were able to decipher the correct four-letter code — "ANCE" — and open the lock.

"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," David Williams, a research associate at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University, said in a statement. "It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!"

The Ann Francis was owned by Francis Shaxton, a merchant and notorious smuggler. Francis claimed the ship was sailing along the eastern English coast from King’s Lynn to Hartlepool, when it was actually traveling in the opposite direction, heading to Spain to deliver a cargo of wheat. Spain was dependent on grain shipments at the time and paid for such shipments in gold and silver from colonial conquests in Central and South America, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The ship was traveling back from Spain to England when, on the evening of Dec. 28, 1583, it was caught in a violent storm. After heading off course, the ship ended its journey in ruin off Margam beach.

A parish register noted the loss of 14 sailors during the same month as the wreckage, which could have been The Ann Francis's crew, according to Amgueddfa Cymru. The deaths were blamed on the nefarious work of a supposed witch.

Locals were quick to loot the Ann Francis wreck before a legal dispute ensued over who had the right to its goods. One Welsh lord claiming the wreck made an inventory list of items he impounded, which included cannons, guns, a piece of mast, Spanish silver and three chests with their locks broken. The newly cracked lock could have originally secured one of these chests, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Centuries after the ship was wrecked, Hughes found the lock near a previously undiscovered stash of Spanish silver coins and coin weights while metal detecting on the beach.

"When I found the lock I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition," Hughes said. "When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief."

Hughes said he attempted to open the lock himself over many years but could never find the right combination. After Amgueddfa Cymru acquired the lock, staff were concerned that they could hear grit moving around inside the dials, and with more than 1,000 possible combinations, they didn't want to cause any damage.

The micro-CT scans offered a nondestructive view inside the lock, and an opportunity to finally identify the correct four-letter combination.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve," Alastair Willis, the senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said in the statement. "Of course, now we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."

#6393. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6391. Engineers created a new tattoo ink that disappears and reappears when you shine different lights on it

Engineers built tattoo inks that switch on under UV light and fade indoors, and the inventor has worn the color-changing tattoo for two years.

A tattoo is forever. That is the whole appeal and the whole problem. About a quarter of people with body art end up unhappy with a permanent mark.

Now there is an ink that stays colorless under the skin until ultraviolet light hits it. Then it turns blue, magenta or yellow in a few seconds, and fades again under ordinary room light.

Engineers at the University of Colorado Boulder built the inks from color-changing dyes sealed inside tiny plastic beads. They tattooed the inks into silicone and pig skin and showed that the three colors can be written, erased and rewritten with light alone.

One person has carried the inks in living skin for more than two years. He is the lead author.

The tattoo itself doesn’t go anywhere. Only the color does.

Carson Bruns of the ATLAS Institute and the Paul M. Rady Department of Mechanical Engineering at CU Boulder led the work, with Mollie Stockton, Emily Gardner and Hyejin Kwon.

The multicolor images were made only in skin models, and the inks have not been through safety testing for people.

In an interview with Earth.com, Bruns put the first caveat in plain words. “First, a PhotoTat is still a permanent tattoo. The pigment stays in the skin indefinitely, exactly like conventional tattoo ink.

What is rewritable is the color, not the tattoo,” he said. “Rewritable does not mean removable.”

Each ink is water carrying beads of PMMA, the clear plastic in plexiglass, bone cement and some dermal fillers.

The beads are a few hundred nanometers across, about the size of ordinary tattoo ink particles. Each one is loaded with a dye that flips between a colorless form and a colored one when light hits it.

The team chose PMMA for a second reason. It bends light almost the way skin does, so the beads scatter very little of it and are hard to see when the dye is switched off.

Three dyes give three primary colors. Mixed in different ratios, they produced a range of shades in a 16-patch test array.

To write a full-color picture, the team switched all three on at once, then erased each color selectively with the red, green and blue light of a laser projector.

“PhotoTat is like a switch. You turn the tattoo on with UV light, but you can turn it off again when you go to grandma’s house,” Bruns said.

Switching the tattoo on takes two to three seconds under a small 365-nanometer UV lamp. That dose of UV is roughly what six to 10 seconds of average sunlight delivers, the team calculated, far below what it takes to redden even the most sensitive skin.

How fast the color fades depends on how bright the room is. Under typical indoor lighting it lasts for hours, but it can persist for days. A bright white keychain lamp pressed against the skin erases it in seconds.

Bruns told Earth.com that mismatch is what makes the system usable. “That asymmetry is what lets skin behave like a display without any power source in the body,” he said.

Sunlight complicates things, because it carries enough UV to switch the ink partly on, even on an overcast day. The team found that SPF 30 sunscreen over the tattoo switched it off completely outdoors in every skin model they tested.

Bruns had a set of black fish-scale outlines tattooed on his shin and thigh. Between January 2024 and January 2025 he filled them with the color-changing inks, more than 30 small tattoos in all. The inks for that pilot came pre-mixed from HYPRSKN Inc., a company he co-founded.

When he assessed the tattoos, 1.4 to 2.2 years after they went in, all three colors still switched on under UV and off under white light.

In one scale he drew a smiley face with a UV pen and erased it. Then he wrote a heart through a printed mask, erased that, and wrote a musical note through a stencil.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him, he named that durability. “I was surprised by how well the PhotoTats held up in my skin,” he said.

Color-changing compounds are known to wear out with repeated switching, he explained, and skin clears and shuffles pigment over time. So whether the inks would last for years in living tissue was an open question.

One person’s leg is not a study of people. Bruns has fair skin, and the authors wrote that a single-subject pilot can’t be generalized to anyone else.

In the lab, the blue dye wore out after 10 to 100 switching cycles and left behind a permanent purple tint that stayed visible in the off state. The authors call that burn-in a critical flaw, because an ink that is supposed to disappear can’t disappear.

Magenta and yellow held up far better over the same number of cycles.

Bruns said his own blue tattoos have so far shown negligible fading or purple discoloration after years of switching. This is different from the lab result that he raised himself.

Two other gaps are built into the chemistry. There is no white channel, so the system can’t make a patch lighter than the surrounding skin. And the blue reads as blue rather than a true cyan, which narrows the range of colors.

The color change also weakens as skin gets darker, for the same optical reason that colored tattoos show less contrast on brown skin, Bruns said. That limit comes from melanin, not from the ink.

Bruns is co-founder and president of MGC INK CORP, which sells a single-color version of this technology as Magic Ink. He is also co-founder and chief scientific officer of its parent company, HYPRSKN Inc.

Two co-authors hold financial interests in both companies, and Bruns is a co-inventor on a related patent assigned to the University of Colorado.

The single-color ink has been through a pilot clinical study of 11 people, published separately in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology.

No adverse events were reported, and the color switching still worked after at least a year. That study validates one formulation, not the three-color system, he said.

Beyond body art, the team sees medical uses. Many people getting radiation therapy are tattooed with small permanent dots so doctors can line up the beam, and most of them report being unhappy with the marks.

“They’re not beautiful, and they become a permanent reminder of a traumatic experience,” Bruns said.

“With PhotoTat, we could turn an involuntary medical tattoo into something that’s only visible to the doctor when you go in the clinic, and then it can be invisible the rest of the time.”

The three-color inks have not been through safety testing in people. Each color has to pass toxicity, sterility and purity testing on its own, Bruns said, and that work is still ahead.

The team also did not look at where the nanoparticles end up in tissue. Their statement that the beads stay in the dermis rests on what is already known about ordinary tattoo pigments, not on biopsies of their own samples. They list that check as a next step.

Clinical studies of the platform in more than one person are underway, the authors wrote. Finding a sturdier blue dye is the chemistry problem that has to be solved first.

Until then, the color-changing tattoo is a laboratory result, one man’s leg, and a single-color product with a different formula.

The full study was published in the journal Matter & Light.

Seeds found in an ancient grave and chemical compounds discovered in mummy hair have revealed people got high on marijuana 2,800 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis.

In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science, researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a "spectral cavalcade," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis, a wild type of cannabis or marijuana.

Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. But it's unclear when people learned about the psychoactive properties of the plant. In the fifth century B.C., the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Scythian nomads inhaled the fumes from burning hemp seeds. And evidence of cannabis use was previously discovered in a cemetery in China dated to about 500 B.C. The new study, however, pushes back this date by three centuries.

Archaeologists found evidence of cannabis use in a burial mound in southern Siberia.

Researchers discovered more than 1,000 whole cannabis seeds and around 500 partial seeds in the Tunnug burial mound, and they carbon-dated them to between 800 and 760 B.C. They also recovered several human hair samples from the grave. An analysis of the hair revealed signals matching cannabinol and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), psychoactive chemical compounds found in cannabis. The tests could not determine how much of the drug people consumed, however.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," study first author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, said in a statement.

But given the burial context of the discovery, the use of cannabis may have had a darker purpose.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," Caspari said. The tradition of human sacrifice, in particular, "would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals," the researchers wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The new study confirms the ancient use of cannabis in funerals in Central Asia and extends the date back to 2,800 years ago, the researchers noted. Future work is planned but will focus on other aspects of ancient cannabis.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," Caspari said. "This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of the crop soon."

Caspari, G., Sadykov, T., Formicheva, D., Blochin, J., Armbruster, D., Happel, O., Ryabogina, N., Boxleitner, K., Spengler, R. (2026). Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago. Science. http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg3800

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6388. A man using a metal detector in Germany found the biggest stash of Roman silver coins from Emperor Hadrian ever discovered

A metal detectorist discovered 934 Roman silver coins near Cologne, Germany, uncovering the country's largest known hoard from Hadrian's reign.

Oliver Riedl had already dug up 15 Roman silver coins in a field near Wesseling, south of Cologne, when his metal detector kept signaling. He immediately notified the regional heritage office.

The excavation that followed recovered 934 Roman silver denarii, about 6.8 pounds (3.1 kilograms) of silver. It is the largest coin hoard from the reign of Emperor Hadrian ever found in Germany.

The LVR Office for Archaeological Heritage Management in the Rhineland (LVR-ABR) announced the find on September 22, 2026.

Riedl, an amateur metal detectorist, was searching the field with official permission.

“For me it was clear that something bigger was lying in the ground here,” Riedl said. “So I notified the office immediately.”

The LVR-ABR‘s branch in Nideggen responded immediately and excavated the site. To study the find more closely, archaeologists lifted it in a block of soil and X-rayed it at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn‘s restoration workshop.

Dr. Erich Claßen is the state archaeologist and head of the LVR-ABR.

“This makes it the largest coin hoard from this period in Germany, and worldwide it is the fifth largest,” Claßen explained.

The latest coin in the hoard was minted in AD 124 or 125. The archaeologists think the coins were buried in the second quarter of the second century, under Hadrian, who ruled from AD 117 to 138.

Most of the coins date to the Flavian emperors, who ruled from AD 69 to 96. Among them is a denarius of Domitian, the last emperor of that dynasty.

The oldest coin was struck in 148 BC, during the Roman Republic. It was more than 270 years old when it went into the ground.

The fortune was probably assembled around AD 100 and buried on purpose decades later.

In that period, the Rhine formed the frontier of the Roman province of Lower Germany. Its defenses, the Lower German Limes, ran about 250 miles (400 kilometers) from south of Bonn to the North Sea, according to UNESCO.

From the late first century BC, that frontier protected the Roman Empire for more than 450 years. Its remains include legionary fortresses, forts, watchtowers, roads and towns.

Dr. Rahel Otte, a research associate at the LVR-ABR, studied the coins.

“At that time, an ordinary soldier in the legion earned 300 denarii a year,” Otte noted.

About half of that pay was withheld for food and equipment. To save 934 denarii, a legionary would have had to set aside all of his available money for about six years, Otte calculated.

Who amassed this considerable fortune remains unclear. The owner may have lived on one of the Roman country estates in the surrounding area.

“We can of course only speculate about the motives, but very probably someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, there were no banks back then,” Claßen observed.

Why the silver stayed in the ground is also unknown. The owner may have died without passing on what they knew about the coins.

The soil block also held fragments of a buried clay pot and remains of straw.

“The coins were probably originally buried in a pot padded with straw,” Otte explained.

Years of farming had destroyed the pot and scattered the coins through the topsoil.

“But in our investigations we were able to find and recover all of the coins,” Otte stressed.

“Mr. Riedl really behaved in an exemplary way,” Claßen remarked. “Thanks to his care, we were able to recover the hoard properly and completely,” he added.

Under the monument protection law of North Rhine-Westphalia, the hoard now belongs to the state. Because Riedl acted lawfully, the state ministry responsible for heritage will give him a reward.

Metal detecting in the Rhineland requires a permit from the heritage authorities and the landowner’s consent, whatever a person is searching for.

Applicants first attend an information session run by the LVR-ABR and mark the areas they want to search on a map. Detectors are allowed only on arable fields, not on meadows or in forests.

Simon Matzerath chairs the West and South German Association for Archaeological Research. About 300 archaeologists from across Germany saw the hoard at the association’s annual conference in Bonn.

“The private use of metal detectors can be an incredible support for science if everyone follows the rules, but unfortunately we also often have to deal with so-called illegal digs,” Matzerath said.

The hoard will go on public display for the first time at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn.

The information was obtained from the LVR Office for Archaeological Heritage Management in the Rhineland.

#6387. The 6 Best Smart Thermostats to Keep Your House Comfortable and Save You Money

Get more efficient heating and cooling with these set-it-and-forget-it models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Just like Wi-Fi-enabled lights and plugs and locks, smart thermostats give you the ability to automate an element of your home for increased convenience. In this case, it’s your temperature controls. These devices tend to be a bit pricier than conventional thermostats, but it’s an upgrade that can pay for itself over time thanks to increased energy efficiency.

Using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely. That comes in handy when, let’s say, you want to warm up the house earlier than usual if you head home from work early. You’re also able to track your usage with monthly energy reports, which can help you bring down your bills.

For the past few months, my colleagues and I have been steadily testing smart thermostats throughout in our homes, including models from Google Nest, ecobee, and Honeywell Home. These are the models we tried, plus a few more we recommend based on our research and reviews. We’ve also included some expert advice on what to consider before you buy.

The ecobee covers the standard lineup of smart thermostat features, with climate control and money-saving that are commonplace among any of the top options, but sets itself apart with a wider range of smart features.

It doubles as a security base for your home security, serving as the arming and disarming mechanism. It also features a built-in air quality monitor that alerts you to poor air quality and sends reminders when you need to replace air filters in your furnace.

The ecobee comes with a separate smart sensor for precision control, allowing it to fine-tune the temperature in the rooms where you spend the most time. Though it comes with a single sensor, you can purchase more to add that precision throughout the house.

It also provides free Eco+ Software which works on your smartphone and generates energy reports that further maximize your energy savings.

The smart thermostat also comes with a host of standard smart features. After connecting to a Google assistant or Alexa, the smart speaker built directly on the thermostat itself can take voice commands and even play music. It also comes with a three-year warranty from date of purchase.

Each purchase comes with a full converter kit as well, so if you aren’t currently in a home with a C-Wire, you can add one by following the kit instructions.

For a smart thermostat that better fits a tight budget, Amazon has its own option that comes with many of the same energy-saving features at a lower overall price tag. Through the connected app, the thermostat tracks and reports your energy usage and peak time periods throughout the week and month.

Through Alexa, you can also set home, away, and sleep temperatures that you can schedule throughout the day and week in order to further maximize savings on your energy bill and optimize your air conditioning to your exact schedule. You can also set the temperature remotely from your phone through the Alexa app.

Beyond the controls, by using an Amazon product, the company will pass along potential rebate and saving opportunities that you could take advantage of by owning a smart thermostat.

As for upfront costs, the device is designed specifically for easy DIY installation so there is no need to hire an HVAC technician unless you want one.

The Honeywell T9 is a great choice if your primary concern is reducing energy use and lowering your bills. You need to pair it with one of Honeywell’s smart room sensors to take advantage of the thermostat’s full functionality, which is an extra hurdle, but the sensor only costs about $30, so it’s a short one.

One of the key ways the T9 saves money is through virtual fencing. Using your phone’s GPS, the thermostat automatically switches between home and away mode as you come and go. So, when you leave your house, energy usage is reduced across the board.

Honeywell also provides monthly usage reports that point out areas where energy can be reduced for a lower upfront cost. Adding more room sensors can increase the accuracy of those reports, giving you more chances to optimize your heating and cooling system.

The Honeywell T9 doesn’t have the same wide spectrum of features as our other recommendations, but it’s core functionality is very solid.

The newest generation of the Google Nest Thermostat has impressed our team as an easy-to-install, easy-to-use option that reduces energy use and is compatible with most HVAC systems. Like previous models, the smart thermostat builds a schedule, learns your temperature preferences, and reduces energy when it isn’t needed.

Reviews Editor Danny Perez installed the Nest in his own home and absolutely fell in the love with nearly every aspect of it. “To say I like this thermostat is an understatement: It lights up when I pass by to show me the interior temps, as well as local weather and humidity (it’s nice to know my presence is acknowledged, not gonna lie),” writes Perez.

Beyond the basic features, Perez also pointed out how much he likes the actual display and design of the thermostat. “Sure, other thermostats and window a/c units have similar smart features, but they don’t blend into my home the way the Google Nest thermostat does. I genuinely enjoy looking at it. I light up when I pass by it.”

With a large, responsive touch screen, this basic Honeywell thermostat is easy to see from across the room, thanks to a large, custom-color display. It’s a versatile option, compatible with multiple smart home assistants. Like other models, it’s Energy Star-certified, which means that using one can help you save even more money through local rebates.

While the smart thermostat is great for easy scheduling and reading, it lacks the learning software of the Google Nest or the virtual fencing adjustments that many other smart thermostats have. That said, it’s also considerably cheaper.

Most smart thermostats aren’t compatible with baseboard heating and cooling systems. This Mysa unit is the rare exception, and designed specifically to work with electric baseboards. Combine that with compatibility across every major smart home system, and the Mysa becomes one of very few thermostats with such capabilities.

While the compatibility alone makes this a tempting choice, it also has many of the same high-end smart features as the competition. This includes virtual fencing, so when you head out for the day, the thermostat automatically reduces energy use.

Another key feature is its temperature monitor. Unlike many other devices, which only provide you with degrees, the Mysa smart thermostat also measures and reports humidity levels.

Traditional thermostats only require power through the four classic wires while smart thermostats typically require low- voltage power all day in order to run the display screen and some basic functions. This low-voltage power comes from an additional fifth wire called the “common” wire or C-Wire. The biggest potential issue you may have with installation is if your home lacks this wire.

If this is the case, it’s probably time to step away from your weekend home project and call an HVAC technician. While installing a common wire isn’t an incredibly difficult undertaking if you’re somewhat handy, it’s one that likely requires the expertise of a trained professional.

Some smart thermostats include installation kits that provide equipment and step-by-step instructions for adding a C-Wire to your current wiring. This can be a helpful addition to the handier among us, and may circumvent the need for an HVAC technician entirely, though you may want to keep one waiting in the wings if anything goes wrong.

Once you've wired and installed your smart thermostat, you can connect it to other devices in your home via Wi-Fi or occasionally Z-Wave. Most units are compatible with many major smart home ecosystems. While they’re compatible with many systems, I would still take a moment to check and make sure that a thermostat works specifically with the smart home setup you use at home.

Along with scheduling heating or cooling programs from the convenience of your phone, there are a handful of features that set smart thermostats apart from their traditional counterparts. Most smart models automatically adjust the temperature based on peak usage and some automatically respond to outdoor temperatures and set ideal temperatures indoors.

Other models use geofencing, or virtual fencing technology. This creates a radius around your home and detects how close or far away your smartphone is from it. With this, the smart thermostat eases energy use when you aren’t home, and ramps back up as you reenter the virtual boundary.

Several smart thermostats we cover use external sensors to expand the reach of temperature readings. Setup is typically no more complicated than placing the sensors around the house and syncing them up with the rest of the system.

They’re great for maintaining different temperatures in rooms, like keeping bedrooms and bathrooms warm and offices and laundry rooms cool. More precise temperature control also increases the potential for saving energy. Smart thermostats that include sensors as part of their systems often come with one, though some models require purchasing sensors separately.

The Popular Mechanics Gear Team has tested several of these recommendations over the course of several months, including the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium and the Google Nest Learning Thermostat. We installed these smart thermostats in our homes, set them up, and used them to keep ourselves warm and cool, as the seasons demanded. We gave them our seal of approval based on ease-of-use, installation process, programmable features, and how well the devices integrated with our smart home assistants, mobile devices, and tablets.

A few thermostats, such as the Honeywell Home Smart Color Thermostat, made the list despite the fact that we haven’t tested them yet. In those cases, we picked options from established brands with the specs and features that are comparable to our tested recommendations, and have received strong reviews from customers at online retailers.

We also prioritized options that were highly compatible with other smart devices and offered convenient features for everyday use. Price rice was a major consideration, as well: We chose models ranging from roughly $160 to $250, ensuring that we recommend a range of options that fit every need and budget.

Tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling. Here at Popular Mechanics, Tom loves testing out home appliances, smart tech, gear for city life and outdoor adventures, small gadgets like watches and multitools, and anything else you can find piled up at his hoarder's nest of a desk.

Prior to working here, Tom attended NYU, graduating with a degree in English and a minor in creative writing. He also wrote for Best Reviews, The Daily Beast, and other publications covering tech, fitness gear, gadgets, and lifestyle products. #6386. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6385. A virus found in one out of ten patients in China is carried by a tick species that is spreading across the US

Researchers in China identified a new tick-borne virus, ALTNV, linked to fever and more severe illness when combined with another virus.

Researchers in China found a newly identified tick-borne virus in 10.4 percent of 3,163 patients they tested. The virus, called Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), also turned up in ticks collected from 15 provinces.

Patients infected with ALTNV alone recovered. Among 38 patients also infected with the virus behind severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), seven died.

The tick species that carried ALTNV most often, the Asian longhorned tick, has spread across parts of the United States. The Chinese study tested only patients and ticks in China, so it does not show whether the virus is present in U.S. ticks.

The work was led by researchers at the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing, with Xiao-Ai Zhang as first author. They reported it in September 2026 in a letter titled “A Zoonotic Orthonairovirus from Febrile Patients in China.”

Their starting point was a gap in diagnosis. More than 30 percent of patients clinically diagnosed with SFTS test negative for Dabie bandavirus (DBV), the virus that causes the disease.

The team screened 3,163 patients with fever and a history of tick exposure. They looked for ALTNV genetic material or IgM antibodies, which the immune system makes early in an infection.

Among patients who had tested negative for DBV, 15.1 percent tested positive for ALTNV.

ALTNV belongs to the genus Orthonairovirus in the family Nairoviridae. Its proteins share less than 80 percent of their amino acids with other species in that genus.

The researchers described 56 patients with ALTNV alone. Fatigue affected 84 percent of them, and 80 percent had gastrointestinal symptoms.

Low platelet counts, known as thrombocytopenia, appeared in 38 percent. Raised levels of the liver enzymes called aminotransferases appeared in 36 percent.

All of these patients recovered without lasting effects.

In the 38 patients carrying both ALTNV and DBV, coinfection was linked to more severe illness. Respiratory symptoms affected 61 percent of them, compared with 38 percent of patients with DBV alone.

Kidney impairment affected 84 percent of the coinfected patients, compared with 66 percent. Seven of them, or 18.4 percent, died.

The two viruses circulate in the same areas and share a tick vector. The authors call for better tests to tell these tick-borne viruses apart where SFTS is common.

The team also tested 47,428 ticks gathered across 15 Chinese provinces. ALTNV genetic material turned up in 1.29 percent of them.

The Asian longhorned tick, Haemaphysalis longicornis, carried the virus most often, at 1.75 percent.

In laboratory experiments, the species passed ALTNV to mice.

Outside Asia, this tick can reduce production in dairy cattle by 25 percent in some regions of New Zealand and Australia, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) noted in 2018.

New Jersey was the first U.S. state to report the tick, on a sheep in August 2017, according to the CDC.

A single female can reproduce without mating. As a result, hundreds or thousands of ticks can build up on one animal or in one area.

Ben Beard, Ph.D., was then deputy director of the CDC’s Division of Vector-Borne Diseases.

“The full public health and agricultural impact of this tick discovery and spread is unknown,” Beard said in 2018.

By October 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture had documented the tick in 21 states, with Kansas the most recent.

There, it was found on a dog in Franklin County, according to the Kansas Department of Agriculture and the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE).

The ticks have been collected from New York south to Georgia and west to Missouri. They are not competent vectors of the bacterium behind Lyme disease, the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) states.

In cattle, the species can transmit Theileria orientalis Ikeda, a parasite responsible for bovine theileriosis. U.S. ticks passed it to cattle in the laboratory, and it has been detected in ticks collected in the field.

In 2025, the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (CAES) reported the first evidence in the U.S. of a longhorned tick infected with Ehrlichia chaffeensis. This bacterium causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis.

Dr. Goudarz Molaei is a research scientist and medical entomologist at the CAES and an adjunct associate professor at the Yale School of Public Health.

“A rigorous program in mitigating risks should include expanded tick surveillance programs, strict measures to inspect animals, plants, and other imported materials at ports of entry, accurate and proper identification of exotic ticks and pathogens, effective eradication and prevention measures, and the ability to test exotic ticks for both native and nonnative pathogens,” Molaei said.

In 2019, an Asian longhorned tick in Virginia was found to be infected with Bourbon virus, the Kansas agencies noted.

The study was published in the journal New England Journal of Medicine.

#6384. Arctic winter sea ice is being overestimated by climate models

Ancient algae preserved in Arctic seafloor mud suggest climate models overestimate winter sea ice, pointing to less ice in the decades ahead.

Arctic sea ice loss usually gets told as a summer story, counting down to the first ice-free summer. Yet climate models disagree most about winter ice.

Together, they simulate nearly a million square kilometers too much March ice – about 386,000 square miles, close to Texas and New Mexico combined.

A new study used traces of algae buried in 6,000-year-old seafloor mud to grade 27 climate models.

The corrected projections show about a million square kilometers less winter ice than before, in every coming decade and under every emissions path.

Crystal Fu of the Scott Polar Research Institute led the work with Matthew Osman at the University of Cambridge, and Marco Aquino-López of CIMAT in Mexico.

The numbers are model projections re-weighted by evidence from the past, not new measurements of today’s ice.

In an interview with Earth.com, Fu compared the missing ice to a country.

“A million square kilometers is a huge amount of sea ice to go missing – that’s roughly 4x the size of the UK,” she said.

Winter ice matters because it’s a lid. Open water in the Arctic winter releases heat and moisture into the air.

That release has been linked to colder winters and heavier snow across Eurasia and North America. It has also been linked to shifts in storm tracks and extreme rain in the Mediterranean.

In March 2025, the Arctic’s annual maximum was the lowest on record.

Yet the models’ biggest disagreements and biggest errors fall in March, not September, and most of the testing has gone into summer.

Fu’s team wanted an exam the models couldn’t have been tuned to pass.

Between 5,000 and 7,000 years ago, a wobble in Earth’s orbit gave the Arctic more summer sunlight. The extra sunlight warmed the region and reduced its sea ice.

The extra heating was comparable in size to what future greenhouse gases are expected to add.

Algae that live inside sea ice leave a distinctive molecule behind, and algae that live in open water leave others.

The ratio of the two in a layer of seafloor mud records how much ice covered that spot. Fu’s team compiled 46 such records from sediment cores across the Arctic, the largest set of its kind.

“What really struck us was just how much information is preserved in tiny traces of algae buried in mud across the Arctic seafloor,” she said.

The team converted the 27 models’ ancient Arctic ice simulations into molecular ratios for comparison with the sediment records.

That let the models be compared with the cores on equal terms. Each model got a weight based on how well it matched, with related models sharing credit.

Weighted that way, the models’ average March ice for the recent past matched the satellite record. The bias of nearly a million square kilometers disappeared.

The range of disagreement shrank by about 6.3 million square kilometers (2.4 million square miles), or 85%. The remaining range was comparable to ordinary year-to-year swings.

The ancient records turned out to be the sharper test. Weighting by the mid-Holocene alone corrected the models more than weighting by 1950 to 1999 did.

The same weights applied to the models’ futures lowered the projected March ice by 4% to 6% for the 2090s, under low, middle and high emissions alike.

Fu noted that the cause of the ancient warming doesn’t change the lesson.

“It doesn’t matter if the warming is natural variation or caused by human activity: if it warms, sea ice is going to melt,” she said.

In the Barents Sea, the Greenland Sea and the Labrador Sea, the weighted maps put the winter ice edge farther north than the unweighted models do.

The shift reaches 5.5 degrees of latitude, about 380 miles (610 kilometers).

Asked by Earth.com where winter sea ice was most vulnerable, Osman pointed to the Barents Sea.

“The Barents Sea, north of Norway and Russia, is probably the place to watch most closely right now,” he said.

The Greenland and Labrador Seas, farther south, are the next places to watch, Osman said.

More ice loss there could affect marine wildlife, shipping, the Atlantic’s circulation and the stability of the Greenland ice sheet, he added.

The projections assume the ice will keep responding to warming the way it did 6,000 years ago and in the 20th century.

The weighting improved the combined projection, but it did not explain why individual models produced different amounts of ice.

Links between winter ice and weather farther south also need confirming. Under high emissions, the weighted models suggest late-winter snowfall over southeast Greenland may be underestimated by more than 30%.

Winter and spring rain in the Mediterranean may be twice what the standard models project, which would raise flood risk there.

Fu said exactly how the Arctic changes will affect Europe’s winters is still being studied.

Earlier work tied a weaker polar vortex and cold snaps to a bare Barents Sea, but those links still need verifying.

Osman said the bigger payoff lies beyond sea ice.

Decades of records of ancient climates can be paired with the right mathematics to test climate models and narrow their projections, he said.

The snowfall and rainfall estimates suggest that ancient climate records could help refine projections beyond sea ice, although those results still need further testing.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

#6383. Archaeologists Found 120,000-Year-Old Human Footprints Where They Shouldn’t Be

They might just rewrite the story of human migration—as a tale of who failed, not who survived.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Between roughly 112,000 and 121,000 years ago, a handful of people walked along the muddy shore of a lake in what is now Saudi Arabia’s Nefud Desert. Elephants and camels had churned up the ground, and the humans left seven footprints among hundreds of animal tracks before sediment sealed the whole scene for eternity. When researchers described the site, called Alathar (Arabic for “the trace”), in a 2020 paper in Science Advances, we called the prints “the oldest-ever human footprints on the Arabian Peninsula” and marveled that they had survived at all. As the researchers noted, an experimental study of modern footprints in mud flats “found that fine details were lost within two days and prints were rendered unrecognizable within four.”

Six years later, the original interpretation still holds. “The age estimate remains about 120,000 years ago based on scientific dating,” Michael Petraglia, an archaeologist at Griffith University in Australia who studies human evolution and dispersal, tells Popular Mechanics. “The size and shape of the footprints are consistent with Homo sapiens.” What has changed is the record around them. Petraglia says sites dated since 2020 suggest that people entered Arabia when wetter weather filled the peninsula with lakes. During these “Green Arabia” periods, people could find drinking water in places that are now desert. When the water disappeared, some of those populations may have disappeared with it, possibly including the people who left the Alathar tracks.

Arabia went through this cycle many times. For a 2021 study in Nature, Huw Groucutt, Petraglia, and their colleagues dated ancient lake deposits in the Nefud that contained stone tools and animal fossils. They found that human ancestors moved into the Arabian interior at least five times between about 400,000 and 55,000 years ago, each time during a wetter spell, and each phase had its own style of stone tools. “This looks like different populations, and indeed species, moving into the area at different times,” says Groucutt, an archaeologist and senior lecturer at the University of Malta who studies human prehistory and environmental change. Once the rains stopped, he says, there probably wasn’t enough water for anyone to stay.

Even in the good years, people probably kept moving. Groucutt pictures groups traveling among scattered small lakes and other water sources in a landscape that was still highly seasonal, with very hot summers. Alathar fits that picture. The researchers found no stone tools or butchered bones at the site and concluded that the lake “was only briefly visited by people,” most likely for drinking water. For Petraglia, that brevity is what makes the tracks valuable. “Footprints capture a moment in time, illustrating that people walked along lakeshores at the same time as animals,” he says.

These walkers may have no living descendants

If the Alathar walkers were Homo sapiens, Groucutt thinks they belonged to a branch of humanity that didn’t make it. “The dominant view from genetics is that people living outside Africa today descend from people spreading into Asia around 50 to 80,000 years ago, so earlier people died out,” he says. By that reasoning, the footprints are “probably an example of an earlier, failed, migration.” That kind of failed migration is also known from other sites, including Skhul Cave on Mount Carmel, where fossils of early Homo sapiens were found. Reaching Arabia, then, came with no guarantee of surviving there. The people who left these tracks may have died out, and a much later migration brought the ancestors of most people living outside Africa today. Petraglia describes the same pattern of shifting fortunes: “Migrations were repeated movements, with groups expanding, contracting, and possibly disappearing from parts of the peninsula as conditions changed.”

As Arabia dried, Groucutt thinks, people may have retreated south, following the water into the wetter parts of the peninsula. Differences in stone tools suggest that these southern populations developed their own ways of doing things as they lost contact with people farther north. But the south eventually dried up too. Groucutt reads gaps in the archaeological record as a sign that the remaining groups became too small and isolated to make it through the worst dry spells. The same lakes that drew people into Arabia could leave them stranded, crowded around whatever water remained and with fewer and fewer places to go. The Alathar tracks date to a dry spell during the last interglacial, which puts their makers in exactly this kind of shrinking landscape.

The proof is hard to find in a hot desert

Settling the question will take evidence that a desert doesn’t give up easily. Groucutt would welcome hominin fossils, though he doubts they would be the “smoking gun” people sometimes imagine, since bones can be hard to date and hard to assign to a species. Ancient DNA could do more, but in low latitudes it “just doesn’t go that far back,” he says, because “hot places are bad for preservation.” Petraglia is hunting for something more specific. “A securely dated human fossil or a long, stratified sequence showing human occupations across both wet and dry periods would be transformative,” he says. Working with Saudi colleagues who help choose sites and reach them, his team is searching around former water sources for evidence of people who stayed as the climate changed.

Until that evidence turns up, the Alathar footprints remain one of the few direct records of these early travelers. If they left no descendants, the site’s name may best describe what survives of them: a trace.
